characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.description: A detective who invites Watson to a unique case and makes deductions during their journey. | The detective who reveals the murderer. | A detective who is examining the ground, comparing impressions, and advising Colonel Ross. | A detective who makes a deduction about the betting odds. | Assisting the Inspector with the investigation, making observations and deductions. | Confronts the trainer, extracts information, and gives instructions. | Discussing the case with characteristic clearness. | Investigating the case, following tracks. | Investigator of the case, decides to return to London. | Investigator, observing the crime scene and questioning witnesses. | Pleased and makes a significant deduction about the dog. | Protagonist, contemplating a case | Sherlock Holmes, who is investigating the case. | The London consultant investigating the case. | The character explaining the essential facts of the case to another person. | The consulting detective, listening to new information about the case. | The detective leading the investigation, making deductions and guiding the search for the horse. | The detective who confronted Silas Brown and deduced his actions regarding the horse. | The detective who has identified the murderer of John Straker. | The detective, absorbed in thought, who later shows signs of having found a clue. | The protagonist, who states he will test the matter on the spot. | The speaker, presenting a summary of facts. | Throwing in an occasional question or interjection, critically evaluating the evidence. | Addressed by Colonel Ross upon his arrival. | Addressed by the Colonel. | Imperturbably watches the race, then reveals the identity of the horse. | Investigator, asking questions about Straker's death.

characters.name: Dr. Watson
characters.description: Accompanies Holmes and observes the interaction with the trainer. | Accompanying Holmes, observes the return tracks. | Companion and narrator, invited by Holmes to assist on a case. | Companion of Holmes, identifies the type of knife. | Companion of Holmes, surprised by his decision. | Companion of Holmes, to whom Holmes explains his findings. | Dr. Watson, Holmes's companion and the narrator. | Holmes's companion and the narrator, addressed by Holmes as 'my dear Watson'. | Holmes's companion and the narrator. | Narrator and companion to Holmes | Narrator and companion to Holmes. | The listener to Holmes's statement. | The narrator, who asks a pertinent question about the stable door. | Made the suggestion that Straker wounded himself. | Mentioned as having described the singular knife.

characters.name: John Straker
characters.description: A man who undertook tendon-nicking, an excellent customer of a milliner under the name Derbyshire, who was in debt due to his wife's expensive tastes. | Believed to have wounded himself with his own knife. | Individual whose boots are found as evidence, implied to be the deceased. | Leading a double life, keeping a second establishment, and accidentally killed by the horse he intended to injure. | Mentioned as 'poor Straker', implying he is a victim or central to the case. | One of the two people who could have chosen curried mutton for supper. | Referred to as 'poor Straker', implied victim, who was brought back to the villa. | Referred to as 'poor Straker', whose death Colonel Ross wishes to avenge. | The deceased man, whose death is being investigated. | The deceased owner of the house. | The murdered individual. | The murdered man, a trainer who succumbed to terrible injuries. | The person upon whom attention now centres after Simpson's elimination. | The trainer of Silver Blaze, who became uneasy and left his house in the rain, later found missing. | The victim of the murder, referred to as 'poor Straker'. | Victim of an incised wound, whose brains were beaten out. | A murdered individual, whose abductor is suspected to be his murderer. | A retired jockey who rode for Colonel Ross and has served him for five years as jockey and seven as trainer, known for being zealous and honest. | Found dead on the moor, head shattered by a heavy weapon, wounded on the thigh, holding a small knife and a red and black silk cravat. | Jockey who rode in Colonel Ross’s colours, then trainer for seven years, zealous and honest servant. Married man, no children, comfortably off. | The individual believed to have gone to the stables at night and taken Silver Blaze for a dishonest purpose. | The murdered man, whose killer Holmes has identified. | The person who was killed. | The victim of a murder that is part of the case Holmes is investigating. | The victim of the crime, whose actions and motives are being explained; wished to take the horse out on to the moor, was leading a double life.

characters.name: Mr. Duncan Ross
characters.description: A character present, surprised by Holmes's daydreaming. | A tall, fair man with lion-like hair and beard and curiously penetrating light blue eyes, well-known, awaiting Holmes at the station. | Addressed by the speaker, has wide experience of turf matters, reacts to the revelations. | An impatient colonel who discusses the horse's Cup entry and leaves for Straker's house. | Employer of Straker. | Initially has a poor opinion of Holmes, later grave and angry about his missing horse. | Leaned back with his arms folded and his hat tilted over his eyes, observing the discussion. | Owner of the horse Silver Blaze, who sent a telegram to Holmes. | Owner of the horse, disappointed with Holmes's apparent lack of progress. | Owner of the horse, involved in the case. | Owner of the racehorse Silver Blaze, who becomes agitated when his horse is not present. | Sender of a letter of instructions found among the victim's papers. | The Colonel traveling back to London with Holmes and the narrator. | The fortunate owner of the racehorse Silver Blaze.

characters.name: Inspector Gregory
characters.description: A character mentioned by Holmes as lacking imagination. | A character who asks Holmes about going to the scene of the crime. | Full of his case, pouring out a stream of remarks. | His attention is keenly aroused by Holmes's deduction. | Police inspector in charge of the case. | The Inspector, addressed by Holmes. | A small, alert person, very neat and dapper, in a frock-coat and gaiters, with trim little side-whiskers and an eye-glass, rapidly making his name. | The competent officer to whom the case has been committed, responsible for arresting Fitzroy Simpson. | The inspector looking after the case, who sent a telegram to Holmes.

characters.name: Fitzroy Simpson
characters.description: A character initially suspected but later eliminated from the case. | A man mentioned in connection to the Mapleton stables, but with no apparent connection. | A person suspected of involvement, whose explanation for a paper and cravat is discussed, and who might have had an understanding with gypsies. | Dropped his cravat during his flight, which Straker later picked up. | A man of excellent birth and education who squandered a fortune and was arrested on suspicion, having placed large bets against the favourite. | A young man who has been arrested in connection with the case. | Individual whose shoes are found as evidence. | Initially suspected culprit in the case, later eliminated by Holmes's deduction. | Suspected by the police of drugging a lad, taking the horse, and murdering Straker. | The man Gregory believes is responsible for the crimes, against whom circumstantial evidence is presented.

characters.name: maid-servant
characters.description: Servant of John Straker.

characters.name: Lord Backwater
characters.description: Owner of the larger training establishment of Mapleton. | Owner of the racehorse Desborough.

characters.name: Master Silas Brown
characters.description: A fierce-looking elderly man, aggressive and unwelcoming to strangers. | A trainer known to have had large bets on the event and no friend to Straker. | A trainer who had large bets on the event and was no friend to Straker. | In charge of Desborough at the Mapleton stables. | Manager of Mapleton, Lord Backwater's training establishment. | Described as a 'bully, coward, and sneak' and an 'old horse-faker' who concealed Silver Blaze. | Initially defiant, then violently started and flushed, later appears ashy pale, perspiring, shaking, and submissive after a private conversation with Holmes. Described as a 'bully, coward, and sneak'.

characters.name: gypsies
characters.description: Roaming inhabitants of the moor.

characters.name: lads
characters.description: Three stable hands working under John Straker. Two went to the trainer's house for supper, one remained on guard. | Two individuals sleeping in the loft who were not aroused by the dog.

characters.name: Ned Hunter
characters.description: A groom who informed Straker of the horse's absence and was later found drugged. | Found under the influence of a powerful drug; later recovers and identifies the cravat and the drugging. | The stable watchman who was drugged and identified the cravat. | The stable-boy who was approached by the stranger for racing tips. | One of the stable lads, remained on guard at the stables on Monday night. | The stable-boy on duty at the stables.

characters.name: Edith Baxter
characters.description: The maid who carried supper to Ned Hunter at the stables. | The maid who carries supper to the stables.

characters.name: tallish man
characters.description: A person of gentlemanly bearing, dressed in a grey suit of tweeds, with a cloth cap, gaiters, and a heavy stick. He had extreme pallor and a nervous manner, appearing to be over thirty.

characters.name: Mrs. Straker
characters.description: A woman Holmes attempts to trick with a false memory. | Provides information about the knife and her husband's friend, William Derbyshire; later questions the investigators about finding the culprits. | Straker's wife, unaware of the expensive dress bought by her husband for another woman. | Wife of Straker, who found him dressing due to anxiety and later discovered the empty stall, missing husband, and drugged Hunter.

characters.name: stable-boy
characters.description: The person for whom the curried mutton was set aside and later drugged. | Victim of suspected poisoning, to whom Simpson wished the maid to give a paper.

characters.name: Desborough
characters.description: A horse, second in the betting, whose owners had an interest in the disappearance of the favourite.

characters.name: Madame Lesurier
characters.description: Creator of a milliner's account for William Derbyshire.

characters.name: William Derbyshire
characters.description: An alias used by Straker when dealing with the milliner. | Customer of Madame Lesurier with expensive tastes, possibly William Derbyshire's wife. | Recipient of a milliner's account and a friend of the victim.

characters.name: Dawson
characters.description: A groom at Mapleton stables, initially unwelcoming but more polite than his master.

characters.name: one of the stable-lads
characters.description: Attends to the sheep in the paddock.

characters.name: Mr. Heath Newton
characters.description: Owner of the racehorse The Negro.

characters.name: Colonel Wardlaw
characters.description: Owner of the racehorse Pugilist.

characters.name: Duke of Balmoral
characters.description: Owner of the horse Iris, which came in third in the race. | Owner of the racehorse Iris.

characters.name: Lord Singleford
characters.description: Owner of the racehorse Rasper.

characters.name: Colonel
characters.description: An interlocutor in the conversation, asking questions about the case. | The owner of the horse, initially skeptical and then amazed by Holmes's revelation.

characters.name: milliner
characters.description: A person who recognized Straker as a customer named Derbyshire.

characters.name: dashing wife
characters.description: Straker's wife, who had a strong partiality for expensive dresses and likely plunged him into debt.

to investigate the case | Location where a special wire was sent to clear up a matter. | Location where the arrested man had come to get information about horses. | The location to which Holmes sent a crimes.name: Murder of Straker and Disappearance of Silver Blaze
crimes.description: A mysterious man attempted to bribe Edith Baxter with money and a piece of paper to be delivered to the stable-boy. | Colonel Ross expresses a desire to avenge 'poor Straker'. | The central crime being investigated, involving the discovery of a body and a knife. | The murder that took place near where gypsies encamped. | The trainer Straker was found murdered, having succumbed to terrible injuries. | Colonel Ross mentions recovering 'my horse', referring to the titular horse Silver Blaze. | Colonel Ross's prize racehorse, Silver Blaze, is expected to run but is not seen, and a different horse appears in its place, causing great agitation. | The central mystery being investigated, concerning the missing racehorse Silver Blaze. | The central mystery involving a horse whose name is being considered for removal from a race due to its disappearance. | The central mystery of the story, concerning the missing racehorse Silver Blaze, whose tracks are being followed. | The disappearance of 'the favourite' horse, which is being investigated. | The disappearance of 'the favourite' horse, which is the central mystery. | The disappearance of 'the most remarkable horse in England'. | The disappearance of Silver Blaze, which is a central part of the case Holmes is investigating. | The racehorse Silver Blaze is missing. | The singular disappearance of the favourite horse for the Wessex Cup | Holmes reveals that the thoroughbred horse was the murderer of John Straker, acting in self-defence. | John Straker's dead body was found on the moor with his head shattered by a savage blow from a heavy weapon and a wound on his thigh. | The central crime being investigated, the method and motive for which are being revealed through the examination of Straker's belongings and intended actions. | The central crime being investigated, the murder of poor Straker. | The central crime being investigated. | The murder of John Straker, which is a central part of the case Holmes is investigating. | The murder of John Straker, whose abductor is believed to be his killer. | Hunter, the stable watchman, was drugged with curried mutton by a stranger to incapacitate him. | Silas Brown concealed the racehorse Silver Blaze at Mapleton to gain an advantage in a race. | Silver Blaze was found in the hands of a faker and disguised to run in a race. | Straker was accidentally struck on the forehead by the horse's steel shoe after frightening it, and then gashed his thigh with his own knife as he fell. | The investigation into the death of Straker, whose body was found in the hollow. | The suspicious death of Straker, which is under investigation and for which an inquest is scheduled. | Straker was found with an incised wound, and the horse Silver Blaze is missing. The police theory involves Fitzroy Simpson kidnapping the horse and murdering Straker. | The central mystery involving events at the Dartmoor training-stables, from which Fitzroy Simpson is eliminated as a suspect. | The favourite horse's stall was empty, and its trainer, Straker, was missing. | The fraudulent scheme to prevent Silver Blaze from winning a race, involving drugging the stable-boy and taking the horse out at night.

objects.description: A piece of matting laid on the ground to preserve evidence at the crime scene.

objects.name: bag
objects.description: A bag containing crucial footwear evidence: Straker's boots, Fitzroy Simpson's shoes, and a horseshoe.

objects.name: boots which Straker wore
objects.description: Footwear belonging to Straker, collected as evidence.

objects.name: Fitzroy Simpson’s shoes
objects.description: Footwear belonging to Fitzroy Simpson, collected as evidence.

objects.name: cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze
objects.description: A cast of a horseshoe belonging to the horse Silver Blaze, collected as evidence.

objects.name: wax vesta half burned
objects.description: A half-burned wax vesta found by Holmes in the mud, coated and disguised.

objects.name: mud impression
objects.description: An impression in the mud, initially mistaken for a chip of wood, found by the Inspector.

objects.name: boots
objects.description: Silas Brown's boots, which had 'peculiarly square toes' and corresponded to impressions found at the scene. | Used by Holmes to compare impressions with marks upon the ground.

objects.name: horseshoe
objects.description: Found by Holmes on the moor, which he puts into his pocket for luck, suggesting its significance as a clue.

objects.name: shoe
objects.description: A horse's shoe that Holmes takes from his pocket to match the impression found in the soft earth, confirming the tracks belong to Silver Blaze.

objects.name: double track
objects.description: Tracks of a horse, initially leading towards King’s Pyland, a key clue in the investigation.

objects.name: return track
objects.description: Tracks of a horse, discovered by Watson, indicating the horse came back from the direction of King's Pyland.

objects.name: hunting-crop
objects.description: A whip carried by Mr. Silas Brown, suggesting his aggressive demeanor. | Shakes in Silas Brown's hand, indicating his extreme agitation and fear after speaking with Holmes.

objects.name: photograph of Mr. John Straker
objects.description: A photograph of the murdered man, requested by Holmes. | Used by Holmes for identification when visiting the milliner.

objects.name: sheep
objects.description: Animals kept in the paddock, some of which have gone lame. | Animals used by Straker for practicing tendon-nicking. | Used by Straker for practicing the delicate tendon-nicking procedure.

objects.name: card
objects.description: A card listing the entries for the Wessex Plate race.

objects.name: drag
objects.description: A type of carriage from which the characters watched the race.

objects.name: spirits of wine
objects.description: A substance used to remove the disguise from the horse's face and leg.

objects.name: thoroughbred
objects.description: The specific type of horse identified as the murderer of John Straker.

objects.name: dish
objects.description: A dish of curried mutton used to disguise the flavour of the opium.

objects.name: candle
objects.description: Needed by Straker to provide light for his intended operation on the horse in the open air.

objects.name: match
objects.description: Struck by Straker to light the candle for his intended operation on the horse.

objects.name: bills
objects.description: Found in Straker's pockets, indicating he was supporting a lady with expensive tastes and leading a double life.

objects.name: bill
objects.description: A bill indicating expensive tastes, which led Holmes to conclude Straker was leading a double life.

objects.name: twenty-guinea walking dresses
objects.description: An expensive item purchased by Straker for his mistress, indicating her costly tastes.

objects.name: milliner’s address
objects.description: The address of the dressmaker, noted by Holmes to investigate the purchase of the dress.

objects.name: light
objects.description: Struck by Straker in the hollow, which frightened the horse.

objects.name: steel shoe
objects.description: Part of the horse's shoe, which struck Straker on the forehead.

objects.name: overcoat
objects.description: Straker had taken it off before attempting his 'delicate task' with the horse.

objects.name: expensive dresses
objects.description: Items desired by Straker's wife, leading to his debt.

objects.name: cigar
objects.description: Offered to the Colonel for a smoke in the rooms.

deductions.observation: The telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart.
deductions.inference: The calculation of the train's speed based on the distance between telegraph posts is a simple one.
deductions.conclusion: The train's rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour.

deductions.observation: Watson asks if the stable-boy, when he ran out with the dog, left the door unlocked behind him.
deductions.inference: Holmes recognizes the critical importance of whether the stable door was left unlocked.
deductions.conclusion: The detail is significant enough to warrant a special inquiry to Dartmoor.

deductions.observation: the incised wound upon Straker may have been caused by his own knife in the convulsive struggles which follow any brain injury
deductions.inference: It is more than possible; it is probable
deductions.conclusion: In that case one of the main points in favour of the accused disappears.

deductions.observation: Gregory's theory implicates Fitzroy Simpson based on circumstantial evidence: his interest in the horse's disappearance, suspicion of poisoning the stable-boy, being out in the storm, armed with a heavy stick, and his cravat found in the dead man's hand.
deductions.inference: The evidence is purely circumstantial and lacks direct proof for key actions, such as why he would take the horse out of the stable, how he obtained poison, or where he would hide such a horse as a stranger to the district.
deductions.conclusion: The case against Fitzroy Simpson is weak and would be easily dismantled by a 'clever counsel', making it insufficient to go before a jury.

deductions.observation: The ivory-handled knife has a very delicate, inflexible blade and blood-stains upon it. Watson identifies it as a cataract knife, 'a very delicate blade devised for very delicate work'.
deductions.inference: The knife was found in the dead man's grasp and is the one used.
deductions.conclusion: It is a strange thing for a man to carry such a delicate knife, especially one that would not shut in his pocket, on a 'rough expedition'.

deductions.observation: A milliner’s account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire, with twenty-two guineas being for a single costume.
deductions.conclusion: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes.

deductions.observation: There was no wind that night, but very heavy rain.
deductions.inference: If there was no wind, the overcoat could not have been blown onto the furze-bush.
deductions.conclusion: The overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.

deductions.observation: The ground has been trampled up a good deal.
deductions.inference: Such extensive trampling indicates many people have been present.
deductions.conclusion: Many feet have been here since Monday night.

deductions.observation: A wax vesta half burned, which was so coated with mud that it looked at first like a little chip of wood.
deductions.inference: The mud disguised the vesta, making it difficult to distinguish from other debris.
deductions.conclusion: It was easily overlooked by others, but is present at the scene.

deductions.observation: The horse is a very gregarious creature.
deductions.inference: If left to himself his instincts would have been either to return to King’s Pyland or go over to Mapleton.
deductions.conclusion: He would surely have been seen by now if he ran wild upon the moor, implying he did not run wild on the moor.

deductions.observation: Gypsies always clear out when they hear of trouble, for they do not wish to be pestered by the police. They could not hope to sell such a horse. They would run a great risk and gain nothing by taking him.
deductions.inference: It is illogical for gypsies to kidnap the horse.
deductions.conclusion: Gypsies did not kidnap the horse.

deductions.observation: He must have gone to King’s Pyland or to Mapleton. He is not at King’s Pyland.
deductions.inference: By elimination, the horse must be at Mapleton.
deductions.conclusion: Therefore he is at Mapleton.

deductions.observation: This part of the moor, as the Inspector remarked, is very hard and dry. But it falls away towards Mapleton, and you can see from here that there is a long hollow over yonder, which must have been very wet on Monday night.
deductions.inference: If our supposition is correct, then the horse must have crossed that, and there is the point where we should look for his tracks.
deductions.conclusion: The track of a horse was plainly outlined in the soft earth in front of him, and the shoe which he took from his pocket exactly fitted the impression.

deductions.observation: A man’s track was visible beside the horse’s.
deductions.inference: The horse was alone before.
deductions.conclusion: A man joined the horse at some point after it left the initial area.

deductions.observation: The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of King’s Pyland.
deductions.inference: The horse and the man are heading towards King's Pyland.
deductions.conclusion: The investigation should follow the tracks in the direction of King's Pyland.

deductions.observation: The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of King’s Pyland, but then the same tracks were seen coming back again in the opposite direction.
deductions.inference: The horse did not continue towards King's Pyland but returned.
deductions.conclusion: They should follow the return track to find where the horse went, saving a long walk.

deductions.observation: The 'peculiarly square toes in the impressions' found at the scene, and that Silas Brown's 'own boots exactly corresponded to them'.
deductions.inference: The person who made the impressions had square-toed boots matching Silas Brown's.
deductions.conclusion: Silas Brown was the one who made the impressions and was present at the scene.

deductions.observation: Silas Brown, 'according to his custom he was the first down', perceived 'a strange horse wandering over the moor'. He recognized it 'from the white forehead which has given the favourite its name', realizing it was 'the only horse which could beat the one upon which he had put his money'.
deductions.inference: Silas Brown saw an opportunity to profit by hiding the horse until the race was over.
deductions.conclusion: Silas Brown led the horse back and concealed it at Mapleton.

deductions.observation: three of them have gone lame, sir
deductions.inference: The lameness of the sheep is a significant clue related to the case.
deductions.conclusion: The condition of the sheep is relevant to understanding the crime.

deductions.observation: The dog did nothing in the night-time.
deductions.inference: A watchdog would normally bark at an unknown intruder. Its inaction suggests it knew the person who was present.
deductions.conclusion: The dog's lack of reaction is the 'curious incident' that points to an inside job.

deductions.observation: The price for betting on a horse has become shorter and shorter, from one yesterday to hardly three to one now.
deductions.inference: Such a significant change in betting odds indicates insider knowledge.
deductions.conclusion: Somebody knows something, that is clear.

deductions.observation: The owner of the horse does not recognize it, stating 'That beast has not a white hair upon its body.' Mr. Holmes, however, remains imperturbable and confident about the horse's performance.
deductions.inference: Mr. Holmes knows the true identity of the horse and that it has been disguised.
deductions.conclusion: The horse is Silver Blaze, and its disguise can be removed to reveal its true appearance.

deductions.observation: Powdered opium is by no means tasteless. The flavour is not disagreeable, but it is perceptible. Were it mixed with any ordinary dish the eater would undoubtedly detect it, and would probably eat no more. A curry was exactly the medium which would disguise this taste.
deductions.inference: By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson, have caused curry to be served in the trainer’s family that night, and it is surely too monstrous a coincidence to suppose that he happened to come along with powdered opium upon the very night when a dish happened to be served which would disguise the flavour. That is unthinkable.
deductions.conclusion: Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case, and our attention centres upon Straker.

deductions.observation: the silence of the dog
deductions.inference: a dog was kept in the stables, and yet, though some one had been in and had fetched out a horse, he had not barked enough to arouse the two lads in the loft.
deductions.conclusion: the midnight visitor was some one whom the dog knew well.

deductions.observation: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze.
deductions.inference: For what purpose? For a dishonest one, obviously, or why should he drug his own stable-boy?
deductions.conclusion: John Straker went down to the stables... for a dishonest purpose.

deductions.observation: The singular knife found in the dead man’s hand was a surgical knife used for delicate operations, not a typical weapon.
deductions.inference: It was intended for a delicate operation that night.
deductions.conclusion: Straker intended to make a slight, untraceable nick upon the tendons of a horse’s ham to cause lameness, making it appear as a natural injury.

deductions.observation: A spirited horse would rouse sleepers if injured indoors, making it necessary to perform the operation in the open air on the moor.
deductions.inference: Straker needed a candle and struck a match to provide light for the operation in the dark open air.
deductions.conclusion: The operation on the horse had to be done in the open air at night, requiring artificial light.

deductions.observation: Men do not typically carry other people’s bills in their pockets, and the nature of the bills indicated a lady with expensive tastes.
deductions.inference: Straker was leading a double life and maintaining a second establishment.
deductions.conclusion: John Straker's double life and financial obligations to a lady with expensive tastes provided a motive for his actions.

deductions.observation: The nature of the bill showed that there was a lady in the case, and one who had expensive tastes.
deductions.inference: Straker was leading a double life, and keeping a second establishment.
deductions.conclusion: The expensive dress was for this other lady, not Mrs. Straker.

deductions.observation: I questioned Mrs. Straker as to the dress without her knowing it, and having satisfied myself that it had never reached her
deductions.inference: The dress was not for Mrs. Straker.
deductions.conclusion: The dress was for the lady in Straker's second establishment.

deductions.observation: It struck me that so astute a man as Straker would not undertake this delicate tendon-nicking without a little practice. What could he practice on? My eyes fell upon the sheep, and I asked a question which, rather to my surprise, showed that my surmise was correct.
deductions.inference: Straker needed to practice the tendon-nicking technique before attempting it on the horse.
deductions.conclusion: He practiced on the sheep.

deductions.observation: Straker would not undertake tendon-nicking without a little practice.
deductions.inference: He must have practiced on something available.
deductions.conclusion: He practiced on the sheep.

deductions.observation: The milliner recognized Straker as an excellent customer named Derbyshire, who had a very dashing wife with a strong partiality for expensive dresses.
deductions.inference: This woman (Straker's wife) had plunged him over head and ears in debt.
deductions.conclusion: His debt led him into the miserable plot.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains Straker's Actions and the Dog's Silence
scenes.description: After Holmes leaves the room, Colonel Ross expresses his disappointment in Holmes's progress to Watson. | After twenty minutes of private conversation with Holmes, Silas Brown reappears visibly shaken, pale, and submissive, agreeing to Holmes's instructions. | Colonel Ross expresses concern about Silver Blaze, noting that his horse's colors have not passed. A powerful bay horse, not Silver Blaze, then sweeps out from the weighing enclosure, causing the Colonel great distress and prompting him to question Holmes. | Colonel Ross informs Holmes and Watson that Silver Blaze is still missing, and they discuss the horse's identity and the unusual betting odds. | Details the routine at the stables on Monday night, including the locking of stables, the lads' supper arrangements, and Edith Baxter bringing food to Ned Hunter. | Holmes and Watson follow horse tracks, with Watson discovering a crucial return track that changes their course. | Holmes and Watson have breakfast, and Holmes, after a day of brooding, announces his intention to travel to Dartmoor to investigate the case of the disappeared horse and murdered trainer. | Holmes and the narrator set off for King's Pyland. Holmes describes his confrontation with Silas Brown, detailing how he deduced Silas Brown's actions in finding and hiding Silver Blaze, leading to Silas Brown's confession. | Holmes explains why Simpson is eliminated from the case, how the opium was administered to the stable-boy, and deduces that the midnight visitor to the stables was known to the dog. He then concludes that John Straker took Silver Blaze for a dishonest purpose, likely related to race-fixing, and anticipates further evidence from Straker's pockets, specifically mentioning a singular knife. | Holmes invites Watson to join him on a unique case, asking him to bring his field-glass, and they prepare to catch a train at Paddington. | Holmes is roused from his thoughts, apologizes to Colonel Ross, and, showing signs of having found a clue, decides to stay at the villa to investigate details rather than immediately going to the crime scene. | Holmes outlines the essential facts of the Silver Blaze case to Watson during a journey, detailing the horse's background and the motive for its potential incapacitation. | Holmes recounts his realization about the curried mutton and powdered opium, explaining how this deduction led him to eliminate Fitzroy Simpson as a suspect in the case. | Holmes reveals his deductions about Straker's secret life, the accidental circumstances of his death by the horse, and his prior practice of tendon-nicking on sheep. | Holmes reveals to the Colonel and the narrator that he has identified the murderer of John Straker, pointing to the thoroughbred horse and explaining it was an act of self-defence. | Holmes, Watson, Gregory, and Colonel Ross discuss the 'singular epidemic among the sheep' and the 'curious incident of the dog in the night-time', leading to Holmes's departure. | Holmes, Watson, Gregory, and Colonel Ross gather in the sitting-room to examine the items found in Straker's pockets, focusing particularly on a peculiar ivory-handled knife. | Holmes, the Inspector, and Colonel Ross discuss the case, with Holmes requesting a photograph of Straker and expressing a desire to speak with the maid. | Hunter confronts the stranger, who flees. Hunter then chases him with a dog but fails to find any trace of him around the buildings. | The Inspector and Holmes discuss the knife found with the body and examine various papers, including hay-dealers' accounts, a letter from Colonel Ross, and a milliner's account. | The Inspector, Holmes, and the narrator are on the moor, where the Inspector finds an impression in the mud. Holmes examines the ground and compares boot impressions. | The characters discuss suspects Silas Brown and Simpson in relation to the disappearance of the favourite while in a carriage, then arrive at a red-brick villa. | The group rides in a landau through the Devonshire city, with Inspector Gregory detailing the case and Holmes interjecting questions, while Colonel Ross and the narrator listen. | The narrator glances at the race card, listing all the entries for the Wessex Plate, including the names of the horses and their owners. | The owner expresses disbelief about the racing horse, while Mr. Holmes calmly observes the race through a field-glass, noting an excellent start and the progress of the horses, culminating in the Colonel's horse winning. | The speaker (implied Holmes) explains Straker's motive for the plot, his alias, and the fate of the horse to the Colonel while traveling on a train, nearing Victoria Station. | This scene summarizes the recovery of Hunter, his identification of the cravat, the drugging of his curried mutton, the disappearance of the horse from the fatal hollow, the discovery of powdered opium in the horse's supper, and Inspector Gregory's arrest of Fitzroy Simpson based on his betting activities. | Watson and Holmes are on a first-class carriage en route for Exeter. Holmes reads papers about the case, calculates the train's speed, and discusses the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze. | Watson asks Holmes about the stable door being left unlocked during Hunter's pursuit, and Holmes emphasizes its importance, revealing he has already investigated it.

scenes.title: Holmes explains his delay to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson why he waited until Thursday morning to take action on the Silver Blaze case, detailing the telegrams received on Tuesday evening, his initial belief that the horse would be quickly found, and his decision to act after learning of Fitzroy Simpson's arrest and the lack of further progress.

scenes.title: Introduction to John Straker's Household and Local Geography
scenes.description: Describes John Straker, his role, his household, and the surrounding lonely country, including nearby settlements like Tavistock and Mapleton. | Holmes and the narrator are traveling, with Holmes commenting on the current state of the investigation and his intention to test matters on the spot. | Holmes and the narrator walk briskly, discussing Holmes' hypothesis that the horse would have crossed a wet hollow near Mapleton, where they should look for tracks. | The maid, Edith Baxter, carries the stable-boy's supper, a dish of curried mutton, to the stables across the dark moor, carrying a lantern. | The pair follow the horse's tracks across the moor, eventually discovering a man's tracks alongside them, and observe the combined trail turning sharply towards King's Pyland.

scenes.title: Encounter with a Mysterious Man
scenes.description: Edith Baxter is intercepted on the moor, within thirty yards of the stables, by a gentlemanly but nervous man who attempts to bribe her with a piece of paper and money for a new dress.

scenes.title: Arrival at Tavistock Station and Meeting the Officials
scenes.description: A stranger approaches the stable window, attempting to bribe Hunter for racing tips on Silver Blaze and Bayard, witnessed by a girl. | After the race, the Colonel expresses confusion to Mr. Holmes, who then leads everyone to the weighing enclosure and reveals that the winning horse is Silver Blaze, disguised by a faker, and that the disguise can be removed with spirits of wine. | Holmes and Gregory discuss the immediate aftermath of Straker's death, the inquest, and Straker's service with Colonel Ross. | Holmes and Watson arrive at the Mapleton stables, where the return track ends, and are met by a groom named Dawson. | Holmes and Watson meet Colonel Ross by appointment outside the station and drive in his drag to the race course. | Holmes and the narrator arrive at Tavistock station and are met by Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory, who discuss the lack of progress in the case. | Holmes and the narrator arrive at the enclosure near the grand stand, discussing the unusual betting odds for a horse, leading Holmes to deduce that someone has inside information. | Upon arrival at the villa, Holmes remains in the carriage, deeply absorbed in thought, observing the surroundings including the moor and Mapleton stables in the distance.

scenes.title: Holmes clarifies the locked door mystery
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson that the boy locked the door and the window was too small for a man to get through, based on information from Dartmoor.

scenes.title: Hunter informs Straker of the horse's absence
scenes.description: Hunter sends a message to Straker, the trainer, informing him of what occurred, which makes Straker uneasy.

scenes.title: Straker leaves the house in the rain
scenes.description: Mrs. Straker finds Straker dressing at 1 AM due to anxiety about the horses; he leaves for the stables despite her pleas, wearing a mackintosh.

scenes.title: Mrs. Straker discovers the scene at the stables
scenes.description: Mrs. Straker awakes to find her husband not returned. She goes to the stables and finds the door open, Hunter drugged, the favourite's stall empty, and Straker missing.

scenes.title: The lads are questioned
scenes.description: The two lads sleeping in the loft are aroused but heard nothing during the night; Hunter is found under the influence of a powerful drug.

scenes.title: Discovery of Hunter drugged and initial search
scenes.description: The harness-room occupants are aroused to find Hunter drugged. Two lads and two women run out to search for the missing trainer and horse.

scenes.title: Discovery of John Straker's body on the moor
scenes.description: While searching, they find John Straker's overcoat on a furze-bush and then his dead body in a bowl-shaped depression on the moor, showing signs of a violent struggle.

scenes.title: Hunter's identification of the cravat and drugging
scenes.description: After recovering from his stupor, Hunter positively identifies the cravat found with Straker and confirms the stranger drugged his curried mutton.

scenes.title: Holmes Summarizes Evidence to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson travel by train, bound for Winchester to see the race for the Wessex Cup. | Holmes presents a concise summary of the evidence and circumstances surrounding the murder of Straker and the arrest of a book-maker to Watson.

scenes.title: Discussion of Police Theory
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the facts of the case, particularly the police's theory regarding Fitzroy Simpson's actions, Straker's wound, and the missing horse. | Upon reaching the hollow, Holmes quickly finds clear horse tracks in the soft earth, which he confirms with a shoe from his pocket, validating his deduction.

scenes.title: Discussion about Fitzroy Simpson's Guilt
scenes.description: Gregory presents his theory implicating Fitzroy Simpson in the crimes, detailing the circumstantial evidence against him. Holmes, however, critically evaluates the evidence, pointing out its weaknesses and unanswered questions, suggesting the case is not strong enough for a conviction.

scenes.title: Confrontation with Mr. Silas Brown
scenes.description: As Holmes and the Inspector emerge from the sitting-room, Mrs. Straker, haggard and eager, questions them about finding the culprits. Holmes then asks her about a past meeting in Plymouth. | Colonel Ross arrives, expresses impatience, and discusses with the Inspector and Holmes whether to remove the horse's name from the Cup entries. Holmes advises against it. | Holmes attempts to question Mr. Silas Brown, the master of Mapleton stables, who responds with hostility and aggression. | Holmes confronts the trainer, Silas Brown, outside, makes a veiled threat, and then whispers something to him, causing a violent reaction. They then go inside to talk privately.

scenes.title: Holmes's trick on Mrs. Straker
scenes.description: Holmes attempts to trick Mrs. Straker by pretending to have met her before, then apologizes and leaves with the Inspector.

scenes.title: Initial investigation at the hollow
scenes.description: Holmes and the Inspector arrive at the hollow where the body was found and discuss the placement of the coat on the furze-bush.

scenes.title: Holmes examines the ground
scenes.description: Holmes takes the bag of evidence from the Inspector, descends into the hollow, and meticulously examines the trampled mud, discovering a half-burned wax vesta.

scenes.title: Holmes and Narrator Continue on the Moor
scenes.description: After Colonel Ross and the Inspector depart for Straker's house, Holmes and the narrator walk slowly across the moor as the sun begins to sink, with Holmes having found a horseshoe. | Holmes and Watson walk slowly across the moor after leaving the Inspector, discussing the disappearance of the horse and Holmes's initial deductions.

scenes.title: Departure for King's Pyland
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson depart, leaving Silas Brown behind, and set off for King's Pyland.

scenes.title: Holmes and Watson discuss the horse and Colonel Ross
scenes.description: Holmes explains his strategy regarding the horse's safety and his approach to Colonel Ross, noting the Colonel's cavalier manner.

scenes.title: Holmes announces return to London to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes informs a thunderstruck Watson of his decision to abandon the Devonshire investigation and return to London.

scenes.title: Holmes announces departure to Colonel Ross and Inspector
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson return to the trainer's house and Holmes announces their immediate departure to London, eliciting a sneer from Colonel Ross.

scenes.title: Departure for Tavistock
scenes.description: Holmes re-enters the room, announcing his readiness to depart for Tavistock.

scenes.title: Encounter with the Stable-Lad
scenes.description: As they enter the carriage, Holmes questions a stable-lad about the sheep in the paddock, discovering some are lame.

scenes.title: Journey to London and Anticipation of Explanation
scenes.description: Holmes, the Colonel, and the narrator travel back to London in a Pullman car, with Holmes promising a full explanation of the Dartmoor events later.

events.name: Holmes decides to go to Dartmoor
events.description: Holmes announces his intention to travel to Dartmoor to investigate the case.

events.name: Holmes invites Watson to a case
events.description: Sherlock Holmes asks Watson to accompany him on a case, highlighting its unique nature.

events.name: Train journey to Exeter
events.description: Holmes and Watson embark on a train journey from Paddington towards Exeter to investigate a case.

events.name: Discussion of the Straker murder and Silver Blaze disappearance
events.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the details of the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze, as reported in the newspapers.

events.name: Holmes receives telegrams
events.description: On Tuesday evening, Holmes received telegrams from Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory, inviting his co-operation in the case.

events.name: Concealment of Silver Blaze by Silas Brown
events.description: A horse race takes place where the winning horse is initially not recognized by its owner, leading to confusion. | A powerful bay horse, which is not Silver Blaze, appears from the weighing enclosure, wearing Colonel Ross's colors, causing confusion and distress to the Colonel. | An analysis revealed an appreciable quantity of powdered opium in the remains of the horse's supper. | An unspecified event that occurred to Silver Blaze, after which he was still considered the first favourite for the Wessex Cup. | Colonel Ross realizes that his horse, Silver Blaze, is not among the horses that have passed, despite the numbers being up. | Holmes and Watson meet Colonel Ross by appointment outside the station in Winchester. | Holmes's deduction regarding the curried mutton and powdered opium leads to Fitzroy Simpson being cleared as a suspect in the case. | Inspector Gregory arrested Fitzroy Simpson, who was found to have placed significant bets against the favourite. | Young Fitzroy Simpson was arrested in connection with the case, but no further progress was made. | Silas Brown found Silver Blaze wandering on the moor, recognized its significance, and concealed it at Mapleton to influence the outcome of a race. | The betting price for a horse has become significantly shorter, indicating that someone has inside information. | The list of horses and their owners entered in the Wessex Plate race is read from a card. | The mysterious man attempts to bribe Edith Baxter with a piece of white paper and money for a new dress, asking her to give the paper to the stable-boy.

events.name: Holmes decides to take action
events.description: After waiting a day for news of the horse's discovery and finding that only Fitzroy Simpson had been arrested, Holmes felt it was time for him to intervene.

events.name: the catastrophe occurred
events.description: A significant, unspecified event that took place last Monday night.

events.name: Edith Baxter carries supper to the stables
events.description: Edith Baxter, the maid, carries a dish of curried mutton to the stables for Ned Hunter's supper.

events.name: Mysterious man intercepts Edith Baxter
events.description: A man appears out of the darkness on the moor and stops Edith Baxter as she approaches the stables.

events.name: Stranger attempts to bribe Hunter
events.description: A stranger tries to offer money to Hunter in exchange for insider racing tips on Silver Blaze and Bayard.

events.name: Hunter chases the stranger
events.description: After being called a 'tout', Hunter springs up and rushes to unloose the dog to chase the stranger, who then flees.

events.name: Holmes investigates the unlocked door
events.description: Holmes sends a special wire to Dartmoor to clarify whether the stable door was left unlocked when Hunter ran out with the dog.

events.name: Holmes sends a special wire to Dartmoor
events.description: Holmes sends a telegram to Dartmoor to verify details about the locked door and window.

events.name: Hunter informs Straker
events.description: Hunter sends a message to Straker, the trainer, about the events that occurred, making Straker uneasy.

events.name: Straker leaves the house
events.description: Straker, anxious about the horses, leaves his house at 1 AM in the rain, despite his wife's pleas.

events.name: Mrs. Straker discovers the situation at the stables
events.description: Mrs. Straker finds the stables open, Hunter drugged, the favourite's stall empty, and Straker missing.

events.name: The lads are aroused and questioned
events.description: The two lads sleeping in the chaff-cutting loft are woken up but report hearing nothing during the night.

events.name: Hunter found drugged
events.description: Hunter, the watchman, is discovered in the harness-room under the influence of a powerful drug.

events.name: John Straker's body discovered
events.description: The dead body of trainer John Straker is found on the moor, with severe injuries to his head and thigh.

events.name: Cravat identified
events.description: A red and black silk cravat found in John Straker's hand is recognized by the maid and Hunter as belonging to the stranger who visited the stables.

events.name: Hunter confirms drugging
events.description: Upon recovery, Hunter confirms that the stranger drugged his curried mutton, incapacitating him.

events.name: Hunter's Recovery and Identification
events.description: Hunter recovers from his stupor and positively identifies the ownership of the cravat.

events.name: Horse's Disappearance
events.description: Hunter's curried mutton was drugged by a stranger, incapacitating him as the stable watchman. | The horse either led to a secret hiding-place or bolted during the struggle and is now wandering on the moors. | The missing horse disappeared from the fatal hollow after a struggle, with no trace found despite a reward and search efforts. | The trainer Straker was found murdered, having suffered terrible injuries.

events.name: Arrest of the book-maker
events.description: A book-maker was arrested in connection with the events, and he volunteered a statement about his presence in Dartmoor.

events.name: Straker's wound
events.description: An incised wound found upon Straker.

events.name: Drugging of the lad
events.description: Fitzroy Simpson drugged a lad.

events.name: Horse kidnapping attempt
events.description: Fitzroy Simpson opened the stable door and took out the horse with the intention of kidnapping it.

events.name: Trainer's murder
events.description: Fitzroy Simpson beat out the trainer’s brains with a heavy stick.

events.name: Initial Case Discussion in Carriage
events.description: Holmes and the narrator reach the town of Tavistock in the evening. | The group discusses the ongoing investigation while driving through Tavistock in a landau.

events.name: Meeting at the Station
events.description: Holmes and the narrator are met at the station by Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory.

events.name: Gregory formulates theory against Fitzroy Simpson
events.description: Detective Gregory presents his theory that Fitzroy Simpson is responsible for the disappearance of the favourite and the poisoning of the stable-boy, based on circumstantial evidence.

events.name: Holmes critiques Gregory's theory
events.description: Holmes challenges Gregory's theory, highlighting the lack of direct evidence and logical inconsistencies in the case against Fitzroy Simpson, arguing it would not stand up in court.

events.name: Gypsies encamped near murder spot
events.description: A party of gypsies encamped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where the murder took place.

events.name: Gypsies gone on Tuesday
events.description: The gypsies were gone from their encampment on Tuesday.

events.name: Moor being scoured for gypsies
events.description: The moor is being searched extensively for the gypsies.

events.name: Stables and out-houses examined
events.description: Every stable and out-house in Tavistock and within a ten-mile radius has been examined.

events.name: Arrival at the red-brick villa
events.description: The group arrives at a villa, which is the location where Straker was brought back.

events.name: Holmes finds a clue
events.description: Holmes shows signs of having found a clue while absorbed in thought at the villa.

events.name: Holmes decides to investigate the villa first
events.description: Holmes expresses a preference to stay at the villa and go into details rather than proceeding directly to the crime scene.

events.name: Inquest for Straker Scheduled
events.description: An inquest into Straker's death is scheduled for the following day.

events.name: Examination of Straker's Personal Effects
events.description: Holmes examines the contents of Straker's pockets, including a significant ivory-handled knife, in the sitting-room. | Mr. Holmes reveals that the winning horse is actually Silver Blaze, who had been disguised by a faker, and demonstrates how to remove the disguise.

events.name: Examination of Straker's possessions
events.description: The Inspector and Holmes review the knife, cork disk, and various documents found with the victim, John Straker.

events.name: Mrs. Straker's inquiry and Holmes's observation
events.description: Mrs. Straker approaches the investigators, asking about progress, and Holmes makes a pointed remark about having met her previously in Plymouth.

events.name: Holmes questions Mrs. Straker
events.description: Holmes engages Mrs. Straker in a deceptive conversation about a past meeting.

events.name: Holmes and Inspector investigate the hollow
events.description: Holmes and the Inspector visit the crime scene where the body was found, discussing initial observations.

events.name: Holmes finds a wax vesta
events.description: Holmes discovers a crucial piece of evidence, a half-burned wax vesta, hidden in the mud at the crime scene.

events.name: Inspector finds mud impression
events.description: The Inspector discovers an impression in the mud, which he initially mistakes for a chip of wood.

events.name: Holmes examines ground and finds horseshoe
events.description: Holmes compares boot impressions on the ground and finds a horseshoe, which he pockets.

events.name: Discussion about Silver Blaze's Cup entry
events.description: Colonel Ross consults the Inspector and Holmes about removing Silver Blaze's name from the Cup entries, to which Holmes strongly objects.

events.name: Holmes and Watson walk on the moor
events.description: Holmes and Watson take a walk across the moor, observing the landscape and discussing the case.

events.name: Holmes discusses the horse's disappearance
events.description: Holmes shares his initial thoughts and deductions with Watson regarding the whereabouts of the missing horse.

events.name: Discovery of horse tracks in the hollow
events.description: Holmes finds the distinct tracks of the horse in a wet hollow near Mapleton, confirming his earlier hypothesis about the horse's path.

events.name: Discovery of man's tracks beside horse tracks
events.description: While following the horse's tracks, a new development occurs when a man's tracks are found alongside them, indicating the horse was no longer alone.

events.name: Tracks lead towards King's Pyland
events.description: The combined tracks of the man and horse turn sharply and head in the direction of King's Pyland, providing a new lead for the investigation.

events.name: Discovery of the Return Track
events.description: Watson observes tracks indicating the horse returned from King's Pyland, altering Holmes's investigative path.

events.name: Confrontation with Silas Brown
events.description: Holmes and Watson question the groom Dawson upon their arrival at Mapleton stables. | Holmes attempts to speak with Mr. Silas Brown, who reacts aggressively and dismisses them.

events.name: Holmes confronts Silas Brown
events.description: Holmes initiates a tense conversation with the trainer, Silas Brown, leading to a private discussion.

events.name: Silas Brown's capitulation
events.description: After a private talk with Holmes, Silas Brown emerges visibly terrified and agrees to follow Holmes's instructions.

events.name: Departure to King's Pyland
events.description: Holmes and Watson leave Silas Brown and head towards King's Pyland.

events.name: Silas Brown's Confrontation by Holmes
events.description: Holmes confronted Silas Brown with detailed evidence of his actions, leading Silas Brown to give up and confess to hiding Silver Blaze.

events.name: Holmes decides to return to London
events.description: Holmes informs Watson of his unexpected decision to leave the investigation in Devonshire and return to London.

events.name: Holmes announces departure to local authorities
events.description: Holmes tells Colonel Ross and the Inspector that he and Watson are returning to London, implying a lack of progress in the Straker murder case.

events.name: Holmes requests Straker's photograph
events.description: Holmes asks for and receives a photograph of the murdered John Straker from the Inspector.

events.name: Holmes plans to question the maid
events.description: Holmes expresses his intention to question the maid, asking the Inspector to wait.

events.name: Holmes questions stable-lad about sheep
events.description: Holmes asks a stable-lad about the sheep in the paddock and learns that three of them have gone lame.

events.name: Holmes's deduction about the dog
events.description: Holmes points out the significance of the dog's inaction during the night, implying the intruder was known.

events.name: Travel to Winchester
events.description: Holmes and Watson journey by train to Winchester for the Wessex Cup race. | Holmes, the Colonel, and the narrator embark on a train journey back to London.

events.name: Discussion of Silver Blaze's disappearance
events.description: Colonel Ross informs Holmes and Watson that his horse, Silver Blaze, is still missing, and they discuss the betting market.

events.name: Holmes reveals the murderer of John Straker
events.description: Holmes announces that he has found the murderer of John Straker, surprising the Colonel and the narrator.

events.name: Holmes identifies the horse as the murderer
events.description: Holmes points to the thoroughbred horse, revealing it as the perpetrator of John Straker's death, stating it was in self-defence.

events.name: Events at Dartmoor training-stables
events.description: The initial incidents that occurred at the Dartmoor training-stables on Monday night, forming the basis of the case.

events.name: Simpson eliminated from the case
events.description: Simpson is no longer considered a suspect due to the unlikelihood of him having powdered opium and the opportunity to administer it.

events.name: Opium added to stable-boy's curried mutton
events.description: The opium was added to the stable-boy's curried mutton after it was set aside, indicating an inside job.

events.name: John Straker takes Silver Blaze from stables at night
events.description: Holmes concludes that John Straker went to the stables at midnight and took Silver Blaze out.

events.name: Discovery of singular knife in dead man's hand
events.description: A unique knife was found in the hand of the dead man, which is expected to provide crucial evidence.

events.name: Discovery of the singular knife
events.description: A unique surgical knife was found in the dead man's hand, providing a crucial clue to his intentions.

events.name: Explanation of the intended horse injury
events.description: The speaker details how the surgical knife was to be used to subtly injure a horse's tendons to cause lameness without obvious trace.

events.name: Discovery of Straker's double life
events.description: Bills found in Straker's pockets revealed he was supporting a lady with expensive tastes, indicating a secret second life and a potential motive. | Holmes deduces that Straker was maintaining a second establishment for a lady with expensive tastes, evidenced by a bill for a twenty-guinea walking dress.

events.name: Straker's Fatal Encounter with the Horse
events.description: Straker, attempting to injure the horse, frightened it with a light, causing the horse to lash out and strike him with its steel shoe, leading to his accidental death when he fell on his own knife.

events.name: Straker's Practice on Sheep
events.description: Holmes deduces that Straker practiced the delicate tendon-nicking procedure on sheep to prepare for injuring the horse. | Straker practiced tendon-nicking on sheep before attempting it on the horse.

events.name: Discovery of Straker's alias and motive
events.description: The speaker discovered Straker's alias 'Derbyshire' through a milliner and deduced his debt-driven motive for the plot due to his wife's expensive tastes.

events.name: Revelation of the horse's whereabouts
events.description: The horse, Silver Blaze, bolted and was cared for by one of the Colonel's neighbors.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.description: A visitor to Watson's room, appearing pale, worn, and highly tense, with injured knuckles, indicating he is in grave danger. | Disguised as an aged ecclesiastic, he reveals his true identity to Watson and explains the ongoing danger. | Giving instructions for a clandestine journey and then departing secretly. | His Alpine-stock is found at Reichenbach Falls, but he is missing, implying he was overtaken by an enemy. | One of the two men involved in the confrontation at the chasm. | Strategizing an escape route and observing the pursuit by Moriarty. | The protagonist, discussing the pursuit by Moriarty and planning their next moves. | The protagonist, who deduces Moriarty's intentions and escape, and advises Watson to return to England. | Vigilant and in exuberant spirits despite the danger, constantly scrutinizing his surroundings. | Watson's friend, who stays at the fall while Watson returns to Meiringen. | Watson's friend, whose non-appearance causes anxiety, but who later reveals himself in Watson's carriage. | Friend of the narrator, distinguished by singular gifts. | Protagonist who visited the narrator, looking pale and thin. | One half of the 'duel' with Professor Moriarty, who is threatened by Moriarty. | The protagonist, Sherlock Holmes, being warned by an antagonist. | The foremost champion of the law, presumed dead after a personal contest with Moriarty.

characters.name: Colonel James Moriarty
characters.description: A man of good birth and excellent education, endowed with a phenomenal mathematical faculty, who wrote a treatise upon the Binomial Theorem, and has hereditary tendencies of the most diabolical kind, pervading London as a criminal. | Antagonist mentioned in connection with Mr. Sherlock Holmes. | Described by Holmes as the 'most dangerous and capable criminal in Europe', whose capture or extinction is Holmes's ultimate goal. | Holmes's arch-nemesis and leader of a vast criminal organization. | The antagonist who has a singular interview with Holmes, known for his soft, precise speech. | The criminal mastermind orchestrating the attempts on Holmes's life. | Brother of the individual whose memory he defends in recent letters. | Engaged in a 'duel' with Mr. Holmes, threatening him with destruction. | The antagonist awaiting Holmes for a final discussion. | Holmes's enemy, involved in the confrontation at the chasm. | Pursuing Holmes and the narrator by train, demonstrating his intelligence. | The antagonist, pursuing Holmes and Watson. | The antagonist, seen attempting to stop the train, indicating he is hot on their trail. | The escaped criminal who is expected to seek revenge on Holmes. | The most dangerous criminal and terrible chief of a gang, presumed dead after a confrontation with Sherlock Holmes. | Won the Mathematical Chair at a university, later set up as an Army coach. Described as having hereditary tendencies of the most diabolical kind, a criminal strain, extraordinary mental powers, and is the 'Napoleon of crime', organizer of much evil, a genius, philosopher, and abstract thinker with a brain of the first order.

crimes.name: Professor Moriarty's Criminal Network

crimes.name: Disappearance of Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty
crimes.description: A personal contest between Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty ended with both men falling into a dreadful caldron of swirling water and seething foam, presumed dead. | The presumed fall of Holmes and Moriarty into the chasm after a struggle on the narrow path.
