deductions.observation: For years past I have continually been conscious of some power behind the malefactor, some deep organizing power which forever stands in the way of the law, and throws its shield over the wrong-doer.
deductions.inference: Again and again in cases of the most varying sorts—forgery cases, robberies, murders—I have felt the presence of this force, and I have deduced its action in many of those undiscovered crimes in which I have not been personally consulted.
deductions.conclusion: it led me, after a thousand cunning windings, to ex-Professor Moriarty of mathematical celebrity.

deductions.observation: The narrator ('I') is fingering something in the pocket of his dressing-gown.
deductions.inference: The narrator is carrying a loaded firearm.
deductions.conclusion: It is a dangerous habit to finger loaded firearms in the pocket of one’s dressing-gown, indicating less frontal development than expected.

deductions.observation: His soft, precise fashion of speech
deductions.inference: leaves a conviction of sincerity
deductions.conclusion: which a mere bully could not produce.

deductions.observation: There were slates and bricks piled up on the roof preparatory to some repairs, and they would have me believe that the wind had toppled over one of these.
deductions.inference: Holmes knew that the wind was not the cause of the brick falling.
deductions.conclusion: The falling brick was a deliberate act of assault, not an accident.

deductions.observation: no possible connection will ever be traced between the gentleman upon whose front teeth I have barked my knuckles and the retiring mathematical coach, who is, I daresay, working out problems upon a blackboard ten miles away.
deductions.inference: The 'rough' was an agent of Professor Moriarty, and Moriarty has ensured that no direct link can be proven.
deductions.conclusion: Professor Moriarty orchestrated the bludgeon attack, but has successfully insulated himself from direct evidence.

deductions.observation: my first act on entering your rooms was to close your shutters, and that I have been compelled to ask your permission to leave the house by some less conspicuous exit than the front door.
deductions.inference: Holmes is in immediate danger and needs to avoid being seen or apprehended.
deductions.conclusion: He must take precautions for his safety and discreet departure.

deductions.observation: Moriarty's men set fire to Holmes's rooms, implying they thought he was there, and the 'bludgeon-man' was arrested.
deductions.inference: They must have lost Holmes's track completely after the arrest, otherwise they wouldn't have imagined he returned to his rooms.
deductions.conclusion: They have taken the precaution of watching Watson, which led Moriarty to Victoria.

deductions.observation: Watson believes they have shaken Moriarty off due to the express train and boat connection.
deductions.inference: Moriarty is on the same intellectual plane as Holmes and would not be baffled by such a 'slight obstacle'.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty will catch them at Canterbury or the boat.

deductions.observation: Far away, from among the Kentish woods there rose a thin spray of smoke. A minute later a carriage and engine could be seen flying along the open curve which leads to the station.
deductions.inference: Moriarty has successfully deduced their travel plans and is pursuing them by train, arriving shortly after them.
deductions.conclusion: The train that just passed carries Moriarty.

deductions.observation: Holmes receives a telegram stating 'He has escaped!'
deductions.inference: When Holmes left the country, there was no one left to cope with Moriarty.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty has given the police the slip.

deductions.observation: Moriarty's criminal occupation is gone, and he is lost if he returns to London.
deductions.inference: If Holmes reads Moriarty's character right, he will devote his whole energies to revenging himself upon Holmes, as he said in their short interview.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty will devote his whole energies to revenging himself upon Holmes.

deductions.observation: a large rock which had been dislodged from the ridge upon our right clattered down and roared into the lake behind us.
deductions.inference: Holmes immediately suspects the rock fall is not accidental but a deliberate act or a signal from his pursuers, confirming the 'danger which was dogging our footsteps'. His actions (racing up the ridge, scanning) and later smile, despite the guide's explanation, indicate this interpretation.
deductions.conclusion: The danger is still present and actively pursuing them, and this incident is a manifestation of it.

deductions.observation: It was the sight of that Alpine-stock which turned me cold and sick. He had not gone to Rosenlaui, then. He had remained on that three-foot path, with sheer wall on one side and sheer drop on the other, until his enemy had overtaken him.
deductions.inference: The presence of the Alpine-stock indicates Holmes did not proceed to Rosenlaui as planned, but remained on the path.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes stayed on the path and was confronted by his enemy.

deductions.observation: The young Swiss had gone too.
deductions.inference: The Swiss guide, who was supposed to accompany Holmes, is no longer present.
deductions.conclusion: He had probably been in the pay of Moriarty, and had left the two men together.

deductions.observation: Two lines of footmarks were clearly marked along the farther end of the path, both leading away from me. There were none returning. A few yards from the end the soil was all ploughed up into a patch of mud, and the branches and ferns which fringed the chasm were torn and bedraggled.
deductions.inference: The footmarks indicate two people went forward but did not return. The disturbed soil and torn vegetation suggest a violent struggle at the edge of the chasm.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes and Moriarty struggled at the edge of the chasm and fell into it.

deductions.observation: The letter from Meiringen
deductions.inference: was a hoax
deductions.conclusion: I allowed you to depart on that errand under the persuasion that some development of this sort would follow.

scenes.title: Narrator's Reflection on Holmes's Activities
scenes.description: Holmes expresses his profound satisfaction and determination regarding his mission to end Professor Moriarty's criminal career, viewing it as the culmination of his own life's work. | The narrator reflects on the modified relationship with Holmes after his marriage, Holmes's infrequent visits, and his recent engagement by the French government, receiving notes from Narbonne and Nimes.

scenes.title: Holmes's Unexpected Visit and Securing the Room
scenes.description: Holmes unexpectedly arrives at the narrator's consulting-room on April 24th, looking pale and thin. He explains he's been 'pressed' and proceeds to close and bolt the shutters, securing the room.

scenes.title: Holmes Advises Watson to Return to England
scenes.description: A tense conversation where an unnamed antagonist warns Mr. Holmes about the consequences of his continued interference with a 'mighty organization', stating that Holmes is in danger of losing his liberty and facing inevitable destruction. | Despite Holmes's advice, Watson remains with him, and they resume their journey towards Geneva. | Holmes arrives unexpectedly at Watson's room late at night, exhibiting extreme tension. He secures the shutters, expresses fear of 'air-guns', reveals his injured knuckles, and urgently proposes an immediate, unconventional trip to the Continent with Watson. | Holmes is attacked by a rough with a bludgeon on his way to Watson's rooms, but he subdues the assailant. | Holmes proposes that Watson accompany him to the Continent to evade the police and the criminal syndicate, and begins to give detailed instructions for their departure. | Holmes's letter explains his impending confrontation with Mr. Moriarty, his admiration for Moriarty's abilities, and his conviction that his career must end this way. | In the Strasburg salle-à-manger, Holmes advises Watson to return to England, citing the danger posed by Moriarty's anticipated revenge. | Watson returns to the narrow path where he left Holmes, finds Holmes's Alpine-stock, and uses Holmes's methods to deduce that Holmes and Moriarty engaged in a struggle and fell into the chasm.

scenes.title: Discussion on Moriarty's Intent and Travel Plans
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson discuss Moriarty's hypothetical murderous attack and their immediate travel plans, considering lunch options. | Holmes and Watson discuss the arson at Holmes's rooms, Moriarty's pursuit, and Holmes's strategy to evade immediate capture by Moriarty to ensure the downfall of his entire organization. | Holmes arrives at Watson's rooms, immediately closes the shutters, and explains his precarious situation, hinting at a 'day of horror' and the need for a discreet exit. | Holmes explains his motive for leaving, fearing he might bring trouble, and then departs secretly from the garden, clambering over a wall into Mortimer Street and taking a hansom. | Holmes explains to Watson his intricate plan to capture Professor Moriarty and his gang, detailing their silent contest. Just as he finishes, Professor Moriarty himself appears in the room. | Holmes, appearing pale and worn, explains to Watson the pervasive and dangerous nature of Professor Moriarty, whom he considers the ultimate criminal challenge, mentioning his recent assistance to the royal family of Scandinavia and the French republic. | On the afternoon of the 4th of May, following advice from Peter Steiler, Watson and Holmes set off from Meiringen with the intention of crossing the hills to spend the night at the hamlet of Rosenlaui. | Sherlock Holmes writes a final letter to Watson, explaining his actions, entrusting papers for the gang's conviction, and bidding farewell before his confrontation with Moriarty. | The narrator describes the terrifying grandeur of the Reichenbach Falls, its torrent, abyss, and the sensory experience of standing near its edge. | Watson finds Holmes's silver cigarette-case and a note (three pages torn from his notebook) left for him near the path.

scenes.title: Holmes reveals Moriarty's criminal mastermind identity
scenes.description: Sherlock Holmes explains to Watson his long-standing investigation into a pervasive criminal force and reveals that he has finally identified ex-Professor Moriarty as the mastermind, describing him as the 'Napoleon of crime' and the organizer of much evil in London.

scenes.title: Holmes reveals the Professor's criminal organization and impending capture
scenes.description: Sherlock Holmes explains to Watson the nature of 'the Professor' as a criminal genius and the 'Napoleon of crime', detailing his vast and cunning organization. Holmes recounts his three-month-long, arduous investigation to expose this network and reveals that he has finally cornered the Professor and his gang, with their capture imminent in three days.

scenes.title: Tense Confrontation and Revelation of Tracking
scenes.description: The narrator ('I') is confronted by a dangerous, professor-like man ('He') who immediately deduces the narrator is carrying a hidden firearm. A tense verbal exchange ensues, during which 'He' reveals he has been meticulously tracking the narrator's activities for months.

scenes.title: Interview with Professor Moriarty
scenes.description: Holmes recounts his singular interview with Professor Moriarty, where Moriarty threatens him and acknowledges their 'duel'.

scenes.title: Conversation with Watson and Holmes's subsequent actions
scenes.description: Holmes discusses the interview's unpleasant effect with Watson, explains why police precautions are difficult, mentions a past assault, and describes going to Oxford Street.

scenes.title: First Attack on Oxford Street
scenes.description: A brick is dropped from a roof on Vere Street, narrowly missing Holmes, who dismisses the official explanation of wind. | Holmes is nearly run over by a furiously driven two-horse van while conducting business in Oxford Street.

scenes.title: Confrontation with Steiler at Meiringen
scenes.description: Holmes arrives at Watson's rooms, immediately closes the shutters, and requests a discreet exit, indicating ongoing danger. | Holmes takes a cab to his brother's rooms in Pall Mall and spends the day there for safety. | The narrator arrives at Meiringen, speaks with Old Steiler, and discovers the letter about the sick Englishwoman was a ruse. | The narrator reaches Reichenbach Falls, finds Holmes's Alpine-stock but no sign of Holmes, and realizes he has disappeared. | While crossing the Gemmi Pass near Daubensee, a large rock falls, which Holmes interprets as a sign of continued danger despite the guide's assurances. | While waiting for a connecting train in Canterbury, Holmes spots a train carrying Moriarty passing through, confirming his successful pursuit.

scenes.title: Holmes's Instructions for Watson's Journey
scenes.description: Holmes provides detailed instructions to Watson for a clandestine journey involving specific modes of transport and timing to reach Victoria Station for the Continental express.

scenes.title: Planning the Escape Route
scenes.description: Holmes explains his elaborate strategy to evade Moriarty, involving a circuitous journey through Europe to Switzerland, anticipating Moriarty's counter-moves. | Watson follows Holmes's instructions precisely, procuring a hansom with precautions, driving to the Lowther Arcade, and then taking a waiting brougham to Victoria.

scenes.title: Watson's hurried journey to Victoria Station
scenes.description: Watson hurries through the Lowther Arcade and is driven by a massive driver in a brougham to Victoria Station.

scenes.title: Watson waits anxiously at Victoria Station
scenes.description: At Victoria Station, Watson finds his 'Engaged' carriage, waits anxiously for Holmes, and assists a venerable Italian priest with his luggage, who then becomes his unexpected companion.

scenes.title: Holmes's unexpected appearance
scenes.description: Just as the train is about to depart, Holmes reveals himself inside Watson's carriage, surprising him.

scenes.title: Holmes reveals his disguise on the train
scenes.description: Holmes, disguised as an aged ecclesiastic, reveals his true identity to Watson on the departing train, explaining the need for continued precaution.

scenes.title: Moriarty's pursuit at the station
scenes.description: As the train gains momentum, Moriarty is seen furiously pushing through the crowd at the station, attempting to stop the train.

scenes.title: Revelation of Baker Street arson
scenes.description: Holmes informs Watson that their rooms at Baker Street were set on fire the previous night, but no significant damage occurred.

scenes.title: Journey to Strasburg via Brussels
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson travel to Brussels, spend two days there, and then continue their journey to Strasburg.

scenes.title: News of Moriarty's Escape
scenes.description: In Strasburg, Holmes receives and reads a telegram from the London police, revealing Moriarty's escape, which greatly frustrates him.

scenes.title: Departure from Strasburg
scenes.description: The narrator and Holmes depart Strasburg after an argument, resuming their journey towards Geneva.

scenes.title: Journey through the Alps
scenes.description: Holmes and the narrator travel for a week through the Valley of the Rhone, Leuk, over the Gemmi Pass, through Interlaken, to Meiringen, with Holmes constantly vigilant for danger.

scenes.title: Arrival in Meiringen
scenes.description: Watson and Holmes arrive at the village of Meiringen on the 3rd of May and take lodging at the Englischer Hof, meeting the landlord Peter Steiler the elder.

scenes.title: Journey towards Rosenlaui and Reichenbach Falls
scenes.description: The narrator and his companion depart from the Grosvenor Hotel in London, intending to cross the hills to Rosenlaui, but with an injunction to visit the Reichenbach Falls.

scenes.title: Interruption by a Swiss Lad with a Letter
scenes.description: While at the falls, a Swiss lad arrives with a letter from their previous hotel's landlord, informing the narrator of an English lady's arrival in distress.

scenes.title: Watson receives a message and departs
scenes.description: Watson receives a message from the landlord Steiler about an English lady in distress, prompting him to return to Meiringen, leaving Holmes at the fall.

scenes.title: Watson observes Holmes and a mysterious man
scenes.description: As Watson descends from the fall, he looks back and sees Holmes gazing at the waters, and then observes a man walking rapidly along the path towards the fall.

scenes.title: Journey to Meiringen and observation of a man
scenes.description: The narrator walks towards Meiringen, observing a rapidly walking man on a curving path.

scenes.title: Frantic return to Reichenbach
scenes.description: Realizing the deception, the narrator runs back down the village street towards Reichenbach Falls.

scenes.title: Aftermath of the Reichenbach Falls Confrontation
scenes.description: The narrator describes the presumed deaths of Holmes and Moriarty in a struggle at the Reichenbach Falls, the failure to recover their bodies, and the subsequent exposure of Moriarty's gang.

events.name: First meeting of Watson and Holmes
events.description: The initial encounter between the narrator and Mr. Sherlock Holmes during the period of 'A Study in Scarlet'.

events.name: Holmes's interference in the Naval Treaty
events.description: An intervention by Sherlock Holmes that prevented a serious international complication.

events.name: Publication of Colonel James Moriarty's letters
events.description: The recent publication of letters by Colonel James Moriarty defending his brother's memory, which compelled the narrator to write his account.

events.name: Holmes's engagement by the French government
events.description: Holmes was engaged by the French government upon a matter of supreme importance during the winter of 1890 and early spring of 1891.

events.name: Holmes's unexpected visit to the narrator
events.description: Holmes unexpectedly arrived at the narrator's consulting-room on the evening of the 24th of April.

events.name: Holmes securing the shutters
events.description: Holmes closed and bolted the shutters in the narrator's consulting-room.

events.name: Identification of Professor Moriarty as the 'Napoleon of Crime'
events.description: A Swiss youth, an agent of Moriarty, is never found again after the confrontation at Reichenbach Falls. | Dr. Watson returns to the scene and discovers the physical evidence indicating the struggle and fall of Holmes and Moriarty. | Holmes arrives at Watson's room late at night, displaying signs of extreme tension and urgency. | Holmes declares to Watson that he intends to conclude his career by capturing or eliminating Professor Moriarty, believing it will free society from the criminal's influence. | Holmes devises a complex travel itinerary to Switzerland, aiming to mislead and outmaneuver Moriarty by taking an indirect route. | Holmes introduces Professor Moriarty to Watson, describing him as a criminal genius and the ultimate challenge to his career, explaining Moriarty's background and pervasive influence in London. | Holmes leaves his current location secretly, fearing he might endanger those around him, and takes a hansom from Mortimer Street. | Holmes receives a telegram confirming that Professor Moriarty has escaped the London police, despite his gang being apprehended. | Holmes writes a letter to Watson, explaining his confrontation with Mr. Moriarty and his acceptance of the potential cost. | Moriarty demonstrates his cunning by successfully tracking Holmes and the narrator to Canterbury, arriving on a train shortly after them. | Moriarty is actively pursuing Holmes and Watson, having tracked Watson to Victoria. | Mycroft Holmes disguises himself as a coachman to help Watson in his escape. | Professor Moriarty unexpectedly appears in Holmes's room, interrupting Holmes's conversation with Watson about his imminent capture. | Sherlock Holmes concludes his long investigation into a powerful criminal organization by identifying ex-Professor Moriarty as its leader, the 'Napoleon of crime'. | Sherlock Holmes writes a letter to Watson, detailing instructions for the conviction of Moriarty's gang and bidding farewell. | The evidence accumulated by Holmes leads to the complete exposure and downfall of Moriarty's criminal organization. | Upon arriving at Watson's, Holmes takes immediate precautions by closing shutters and planning a discreet exit, highlighting the pervasive threat. | Watson discovers Holmes's silver cigarette-case and a note (three pages torn from his note-book) left for him. | Watson follows Holmes's detailed instructions for a secret journey, involving a hansom and a brougham, to reach Victoria Station.

events.name: Holmes Secures Shutters
events.description: A large rock falls near Holmes and the narrator while crossing the Gemmi Pass, which Holmes perceives as an intentional act or a sign of their pursuers. | Holmes quickly and securely bolts the shutters in Watson's room, expressing fear of 'air-guns'. | Holmes shows Watson his burst and bleeding knuckles, indicating a recent physical struggle.

events.name: Holmes's Plan to Capture Moriarty's Gang
events.description: An unnamed antagonist confronts Mr. Holmes, detailing the timeline of Holmes's interference and issuing a grave warning about the 'mighty organization' he is opposing, urging him to withdraw. | Holmes and Watson continue their journey towards Geneva, with Watson choosing to remain with Holmes despite the increased danger. | Holmes and the narrator travel from Strasburg through various Alpine locations to Meiringen, constantly aware of a looming threat. | Holmes decides against arresting Moriarty immediately, preferring to wait to capture his entire criminal network. | Holmes reveals his elaborate plan to capture Professor Moriarty and all principal members of his gang within three days, leading to the greatest criminal trial of the century. | Holmes urgently proposes that Watson accompany him on an immediate, aimless trip to the Continent. | Holmes warns Watson of the extreme danger they face from Moriarty's revenge and advises him to return to England for his safety. | The narrator and his companion make a detour to see the Reichenbach Falls as instructed. | The narrator rushes back to Reichenbach Falls after realizing the deception of the letter.

events.name: Holmes's investigation of the Professor's organization
events.description: Holmes devoted his entire energy to deducing, exposing, and breaking up the Professor's criminal organization, facing an antagonist who was his intellectual equal for three months.

events.name: Imminent capture of the Professor and his gang
events.description: Holmes has successfully woven his 'net' around the Professor and his principal gang members, and their capture by the police is expected in three days, on the upcoming Monday.

events.name: Confrontation with 'He'
events.description: The narrator ('I') faces a dangerous individual ('He') who deduces the presence of a hidden weapon and reveals he has been tracking the narrator's movements.

events.name: Singular interview with Professor Moriarty
events.description: Holmes has a private meeting with Professor Moriarty where they discuss their ongoing conflict and exchange threats.

events.name: Holmes's past assault
events.description: Holmes mentions to Watson that he has already been assaulted, implying Moriarty's agents were responsible.

events.name: Holmes goes to Oxford Street
events.description: Holmes goes out about midday to transact some business in Oxford Street.

events.name: Holmes Instructs Watson on Clandestine Travel
events.description: A brick is dropped from a roof on Vere Street, narrowly missing Holmes, confirming a second deliberate attempt on his life. | A two-horse van attempts to run over Holmes on Oxford Street, marking the first attempt on his life. | Holmes gives Watson precise instructions for a secret journey to Victoria Station to catch the Continental express. | Holmes is attacked by a rough with a bludgeon on his way to Watson's, representing a third attempt on his life.

events.name: Holmes closes shutters
events.description: Holmes's first act upon entering Watson's rooms is to close the shutters for security.

events.name: Holmes invites Watson to the Continent
events.description: Holmes asks Watson to join him on a trip to the Continent to escape immediate danger.

events.name: Instructions for departure
events.description: Holmes gives Watson detailed instructions for dispatching luggage and taking a hansom cab to a specific location.

events.name: Watson's departure preparation
events.description: Watson travels to Victoria Station to catch a train, expecting to meet Holmes there for their journey.

events.name: Holmes's unexpected arrival
events.description: Holmes, after causing Watson anxiety by his absence, reveals himself to be already inside Watson's train carriage just before departure.

events.name: Holmes's disguise revelation
events.description: Holmes, previously disguised as an aged ecclesiastic, reveals his true identity to Watson on the train.

events.name: Moriarty's failed attempt to stop the train
events.description: Professor Moriarty is seen attempting to stop the departing train, confirming Holmes's suspicion that they are being pursued.

events.name: Baker Street rooms set on fire
events.description: Holmes informs Watson that their rooms at Baker Street were set on fire the previous night by their adversaries.

events.name: Arson at Holmes's rooms
events.description: Moriarty's men set fire to Holmes's rooms the previous night, though no great harm was done.

events.name: Confrontation at Reichenbach Falls
events.description: Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty engage in a personal contest at the Reichenbach Falls, resulting in both men reeling over and their presumed deaths. | The struggle between Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty on the narrow path above the chasm, leading to their presumed fall. | Watson and Holmes reach the village of Meiringen on the 3rd of May and check into the Englischer Hof.

events.name: Departure for Rosenlaui
events.description: On the 4th of May, Watson and Holmes depart from Meiringen, heading towards the hamlet of Rosenlaui.

events.name: Departure from Grosvenor Hotel
events.description: The narrator and his companion set off from the Grosvenor Hotel on the afternoon of the 4th.

events.name: Receipt of a letter at Reichenbach Falls
events.description: A Swiss lad delivers a letter to the narrator while he is at the Reichenbach Falls.

events.name: Arrival of an English lady at the hotel
events.description: An English lady, in the last stage of consumption, arrives at the hotel shortly after the narrator and his companion left.

events.name: Watson receives a message about an English lady
events.description: A message arrives from the landlord Steiler, requesting Watson's return to attend to a dying English lady.

events.name: Watson agrees to return to Meiringen
events.description: Watson, despite his scruples about leaving Holmes, agrees to return to Meiringen to attend to the English lady.

events.name: Watson leaves Holmes at the fall
events.description: Watson departs from Holmes, who remains at the fall with a young Swiss messenger, planning to walk to Rosenlaui later.

events.name: Watson observes a man walking rapidly towards the fall
events.description: As Watson descends, he looks back and sees a man walking very rapidly along the path leading to the fall.

events.name: Deceptive letter received
events.description: The narrator receives a letter falsely claiming a sick Englishwoman at Steiler's hotel, luring him away from Holmes.

events.name: Discovery of Holmes's disappearance
events.description: The narrator finds Holmes's Alpine-stock at Reichenbach Falls but Holmes is gone, implying he was overtaken by an enemy.

events.name: Holmes's Confrontation with Moriarty
events.description: Holmes awaits Mr. Moriarty for a 'final discussion' regarding their conflict.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.description: A brilliant detective, reclusive, uses cocaine, and deeply attracted to the study of crime. | A tall, spare figure, pacing swiftly and eagerly, engrossed in a new problem. | An acute reasoner and fine actor who disguises himself as an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman. | Analyzing a note and awaiting a client, demonstrating his deductive skills. | Changed his costume; his expression, manner, and soul seemed to vary with every fresh part he assumed; an acute reasoner. | Consulted by Your Majesty regarding a delicate matter. | Consulting detective, listening to the King's problem. | Consulting detective, planning the retrieval of a photograph. | One of the hosts, addressed by the visitor regarding a sensitive case. | Protagonist, injured during a staged scuffle in the street. | The detective who receives the visitor. | The detective, explaining his deductions. | The detective, feigning injury as part of a ruse to locate a photograph. | The detective, who is analyzing the mysterious note and making deductions. | The most incisive reasoner and most energetic agent in Europe, initially appearing languid and lounging. | The protagonist, known for his masterly grasp of situations and keen reasoning. He returns to Baker Street disguised as a drunken-looking groom before changing into respectable tweed. | Sherlock Holmes, identifying himself. | The consulting detective, reacting with chagrin and surprise. | The protagonist, investigating the case for the King of Bohemia. | the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, with a cold, precise but admirably balanced mind, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian | The consulting detective, surprised by Irene Adler's departure. | The detective whose plans were beaten by a woman's wit. | The recipient of Irene Adler's letter, who was outwitted by her. | The recipient of Irene Norton's letter, who makes a cold remark about the King's level and requests Irene's photograph as a reward.

characters.description: A well-known adventuress, contralto, and prima donna, entangled with Your Majesty. | Subject of the investigation, described as daintiest and sings at concerts. | The bride who marries Godfrey Norton and gives the narrator a sovereign. | The lady involved in the scuffle, who allows Holmes to be brought into her home. | The woman who possesses a compromising photograph of the King, now revealed to be married. | The woman who possesses the compromising photograph and threatens to send it. | The woman who wrote the letter, describing how she outwitted Holmes and fled. | The woman whose photograph is found. | The woman whose wit defeated Holmes's plans, referred to by Holmes as 'the woman'. | the woman who eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex in Holmes's eyes, of dubious and questionable memory | A woman whose photograph is central to the scandal. | Subject of the investigation, described as daintiest and sings at concerts. | The subject of Holmes's investigation, whose habits and house were being watched. | The woman they plan to meet at Briony Lodge; also referred to as Madame.

crimes.name: Irene Adler's Evasion and Retention of the Photograph
crimes.description: A delicate matter that could seriously compromise the reigning family of Bohemia, the House of Ormstein. | A great scandal threatening the kingdom of Bohemia, centered around Irene Adler's photograph. | A matter of extreme importance that could lead to an immense scandal and seriously compromise one of the reigning families of Europe, specifically the House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia. | An inquiry Holmes is conducting for a client of exalted station, which the narrator finds deeply interesting. | Holmes and Watson are attempting to determine the identity and intentions of a German individual who sent a note written on Bohemian paper, before the client even enters. | Holmes spent the morning watching the habits and house of Miss Irene Adler, disguised as a groom, as part of an ongoing inquiry. | Irene Adler possesses compromising letters from Your Majesty and might use them for blackmail or other purposes. | Irene Adler successfully evades Sherlock Holmes's attempt to retrieve a compromising photograph and leaves the country, keeping the photograph for her own safeguard against the King. | The King of Bohemia's 'business' was to retrieve a compromising photograph of himself and Irene Norton. Irene's letter resolves this by stating she will keep it for self-safeguard but leaves another photograph for the King. | The King's fear that Irene Adler will use a photograph to interfere with his plans or expose his past affair. | The King's multiple failed attempts to recover a compromising photograph from Irene Adler, involving burglars, luggage diversion, and waylaying. | The central mystery involves retrieving a compromising photograph from Miss Adler, with Mr. Godfrey Norton potentially involved in its safekeeping. | The central quest to retrieve a compromising photograph from 'our lady of to-day'. | The central mystery revolves around a photograph and the relationship between the gentleman and the woman, influencing the direction of the investigation. | The central mystery revolves around the location and concealment of a compromising photograph, which the King wants to retrieve and the woman (implied Irene Adler) wants to keep hidden from Mr. Godfrey Norton and the King's fiancée. Two attempts to waylay and search her for it have already been made. | The underlying threat of exposing the King of Bohemia through a compromising photograph, which Holmes is attempting to prevent by locating the photograph.

deductions.observation: you have put on seven and a half pounds since I saw you.
deductions.inference: Weight gain and a settled appearance often accompany a comfortable, married life.
deductions.conclusion: Wedlock suits you.

deductions.observation: in practice again, I observe.
deductions.inference: Watson's demeanor, attire, or perhaps a specific item he carries indicates his return to his medical profession.
deductions.conclusion: Watson has returned to his medical practice.

deductions.observation: you have been getting yourself very wet lately
deductions.inference: There are subtle signs on Watson's clothing or person indicating recent exposure to moisture.
deductions.conclusion: Watson has recently been out in wet conditions.

deductions.observation: you have a most clumsy and careless servant girl
deductions.inference: Minor imperfections or marks on Watson's clothing or belongings suggest a servant's lack of care.
deductions.conclusion: Watson employs a clumsy and careless servant girl.

deductions.observation: on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it, the leather is scored by six almost parallel cuts.
deductions.inference: they have been caused by someone who has very carelessly scraped round the edges of the sole in order to remove crusted mud from it.
deductions.conclusion: you had been out in vile weather, and that you had a particularly malignant boot-slitting specimen of the London slavey.

deductions.observation: a gentleman walks into my rooms smelling of iodoform, with a black mark of nitrate of silver upon his right forefinger, and a bulge on the right side of his top-hat to show where he has secreted his stethoscope
deductions.inference: These specific observations are characteristic signs of a medical professional.
deductions.conclusion: an active member of the medical profession.

deductions.observation: You have frequently seen the steps which lead up from the hall to this room.
deductions.inference: You see, but you do not observe. You have not observed how many steps there are.
deductions.conclusion: I know that there are seventeen steps, because I have both seen and observed.

deductions.observation: The paper upon which the note was written could not be bought under half a crown a packet. It is peculiarly strong and stiff.
deductions.inference: Such paper is expensive.
deductions.conclusion: The man who wrote it was presumably well to do.

deductions.observation: The paper is peculiarly strong and stiff.
deductions.inference: This quality is not typical of English paper.
deductions.conclusion: It is not an English paper at all.

deductions.observation: A large 'E' with a small 'g,' a 'P,' and a large 'G' with a small 't' woven into the texture of the paper.
deductions.inference: The 'G' with the small 't' stands for 'Gesellschaft' (German for 'Company'), and 'P' stands for 'Papier'. The 'Eg' likely refers to a place.
deductions.conclusion: The paper is German and likely from a specific location starting with 'Eg'.

deductions.observation: The initials 'Eg' on the paper, combined with a search in the Continental Gazetteer.
deductions.inference: The Gazetteer lists 'Egria' as a relevant location.
deductions.conclusion: The paper comes from Egria, a German-speaking country in Bohemia, known for its paper-mills.

deductions.observation: The paper was made in Bohemia, and the sentence construction ('This account of you we have from all quarters received') is peculiar, uncourteous to its verbs.
deductions.inference: The paper's origin and the grammatical structure point to a specific nationality.
deductions.conclusion: The man who wrote the note is a German.

deductions.observation: The sharp sound of horses’ hoofs and grating wheels against the curb, followed by a sharp pull at the bell, indicates a pair of horses and a brougham.
deductions.inference: A brougham with a pair of horses, valued at 'a hundred and fifty guineas apiece', suggests considerable wealth.
deductions.conclusion: There’s money in this case.

deductions.observation: The nature of the case involving a reigning European family, specifically the House of Ormstein, combined with the client's 'gigantic' stature and initial demeanor.
deductions.inference: Holmes connected these observations with his extensive knowledge of European royalty and the specific individuals involved in such high-stakes matters.
deductions.conclusion: The visitor is Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia.

deductions.observation: There is the writing.
deductions.inference: The writing proves authenticity.
deductions.conclusion: Forgery.

deductions.observation: My private note-paper.
deductions.inference: The paper proves authenticity.
deductions.conclusion: Stolen.

deductions.observation: My own seal.
deductions.inference: The seal proves authenticity.
deductions.conclusion: Imitated.

deductions.observation: My photograph.
deductions.inference: The photograph proves authenticity.
deductions.conclusion: Bought.

deductions.observation: We were both in the photograph.
deductions.inference: This is undeniable proof of their relationship and the photograph's authenticity.
deductions.conclusion: Your Majesty has indeed committed an indiscretion.

deductions.observation: this marriage rather simplifies matters.
deductions.inference: The photograph becomes a double-edged weapon now.
deductions.conclusion: The chances are that she would be as averse to its being seen by Mr. Godfrey Norton, as our client is to its coming to the eyes of his princess.

deductions.observation: It is most unlikely that she carries it about with her. It is cabinet size. Too large for easy concealment about a woman’s dress. She knows that the King is capable of having her waylaid and searched. Two attempts of the sort have already been made.
deductions.conclusion: We may take it, then, that she does not carry it about with her.

deductions.observation: The object is too large for easy concealment about a woman’s dress. She knows that the King is capable of having her waylaid and searched. Two attempts of the sort have already been made.
deductions.inference: She does not carry it about with her.
deductions.conclusion: It must be in her own house.

deductions.observation: Her house has twice been burgled in search of the object.
deductions.inference: The burglars did not know how to look.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes will get her to show him the object, implying his method will succeed where others failed.

deductions.observation: everyone in the street was an accomplice. They were all engaged for the evening.
deductions.inference: The uproar was a staged event, and the crowd was part of the plan.
deductions.conclusion: The situation was orchestrated to allow Holmes to execute his trick.

deductions.observation: When a woman thinks that her house is on fire, her instinct is at once to rush to the thing which she values most.
deductions.inference: This is a perfectly overpowering impulse that can be exploited.
deductions.conclusion: By simulating a fire, the woman would instinctively reveal the hiding place of the photograph.

deductions.observation: her instinct is at once to rush to the thing which she values most.
deductions.inference: our lady of to-day had nothing in the house more precious to her than what we are in quest of. She would rush to secure it.
deductions.conclusion: A simulated fire alarm would cause her to reveal the hiding place of the photograph.

deductions.observation: She was there in an instant, and I caught a glimpse of it as she half drew it out.
deductions.inference: Her immediate action upon the alarm revealed the location.
deductions.conclusion: The photograph is in a recess behind a sliding panel just above the right bell-pull.

scenes.title: Introduction to Sherlock Holmes and Irene Adler
scenes.description: The narrator introduces Sherlock Holmes's unique character, his aversion to emotions, and his singular regard for Irene Adler, explaining their past relationship and the narrator's recent absence due to marriage.

scenes.title: Holmes's Reclusive Life and Past Triumphs
scenes.description: Holmes declares a false alarm. Watson slips away through the crowd and meets Holmes at the corner of the street. | Immediately after the wedding, Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton separate at the church door, driving off in different directions. Irene Adler states her intention to drive in the park at five. | The King of Bohemia explains his predicament to Holmes, detailing his past indiscretion with Irene Adler, the existence of a compromising photograph, his impending marriage to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, and Irene Adler's threat to send the photograph. He also recounts his five failed attempts to recover the photograph. | The narrator reflects on Holmes's reclusive, Bohemian nature, his use of cocaine, and his dedication to solving crimes, mentioning past cases like the Trepoff murder, the Atkinson brothers' tragedy, and a mission for the Holland family. | Watson is shown into Holmes's chamber, where Holmes, after a brief greeting, offers him cigars and drinks, then proceeds to make several astute deductions about Watson's recent life.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains Deductions to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes and the narrator discuss the plan to visit Irene Adler at 8 AM. Holmes is recognized by a passing youth on Baker Street. | Holmes explains to Watson how he deduced Watson's recent country walk and the carelessness of his servant girl, then provides a hypothetical example of deducing a doctor's profession. | On March 20, 1888, the narrator returns from a patient visit, passing Baker Street, and feels a strong desire to visit Holmes upon seeing his brightly lit rooms.

scenes.title: The Visitor's Arrival and Introduction of the Scandal
scenes.description: A mysterious visitor with a German accent, identifying himself as Count Von Kramm, arrives to consult Holmes and Watson about a matter of extreme importance involving a potential scandal for the House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia. He requests absolute secrecy from both. | The King of Bohemia rushes into Holmes's rooms at Baker Street, eager for news. Holmes reveals Irene Adler's marriage to Norton. | Watson arrives at Holmes's residence, observes Holmes pacing in his brilliantly lit rooms, and rings the bell to enter.

scenes.title: Discussion on Observation and the Steps
scenes.description: Holmes explains the difference between merely seeing and actively observing, using the example of the steps leading to their room.

scenes.title: Planning the Retrieval of the Photograph
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson are interrupted by the arrival of a very tall, richly dressed man with a German accent, wearing a vizard mask. | Holmes and Watson examine a mysterious note, with Holmes making detailed deductions about the paper's origin based on its quality and watermarks, leading them to identify Egria in Bohemia. | Holmes presents a recently arrived, anonymous, undated note to the narrator, asking him to read it aloud. | Holmes, the King, and Watson discuss the timeline for the photograph's disclosure, the payment for Holmes's services, and obtain Mademoiselle's address. | Immediately after the gentleman's departure, a landau arrives up the lane, driven by a disheveled coachman. | Mr. Sherlock Holmes, the King of Bohemia, and a third person (implied Watson) read Irene Norton's letter, which details her decision to keep the compromising photograph for her own protection but also leaves another photograph for the King. The King expresses his admiration for Irene and his satisfaction with the outcome. Holmes declines a monetary reward, instead requesting Irene's photograph, which the King grants. | The narrator reads the note, which announces a visit from a gentleman at a quarter to eight, seeking consultation on a matter of great importance, and mentions the visitor might wear a mask.

scenes.title: Holmes and Watson Discuss the German's Note and Await the Client
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson analyze the origin and grammar of a mysterious note, deducing the writer is German. They then hear the arrival of their client, whom Holmes anticipates will resolve their doubts.

scenes.title: The King of Bohemia reveals his identity
scenes.description: Holmes and the visitor discuss the delicate matter implicating the House of Ormstein. The visitor, initially disguised, becomes agitated and reveals himself to be Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, the King of Bohemia. He explains his incognito visit from Prague to consult Holmes.

scenes.title: The Ruse Begins: Holmes's Feigned Injury
scenes.description: A woman quickly enters a landau, instructing her coachman, John, to drive urgently to the Church of St. Monica, offering a half sovereign for speed. | Holmes emerges from his bedroom, dressed, and laughs heartily by the fire, expressing amusement about his morning's activities to the narrator. | Holmes is carried into Briony Lodge, feigning injury, while Watson observes from a window. Watson reflects on the deception and his role. | Holmes retreats to his bedroom and returns transformed into an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman for his new role. | Holmes returns to Baker Street disguised as a drunken-looking groom. He quickly retreats to his bedroom to change into respectable clothes, then relaxes by the fire, laughing heartily. | Holmes, with his eyes shut, listens as Your Majesty explains his past entanglement with Irene Adler in Warsaw, the compromising letters, and his urgent need to retrieve them to prevent blackmail. Holmes questions the King about the details and the authenticity of the potential evidence. | Irene Adler, the lady Holmes protected, observes his injury from the top of the steps and allows him to be brought into Briony Lodge. | Sherlock Holmes, Watson, and the King read Irene Adler's letter, in which she reveals how she saw through Holmes's disguise, followed him, and then fled with her husband, taking the compromising photograph with her. | The gentleman emerges from Briony Lodge, looking flurried, checks his gold watch, and instructs the cabman to drive quickly to Gross & Hankey's and then to the Church of St. Monica. | The gentleman is observed through the windows of the sitting-room, pacing, talking excitedly, and waving his arms for about half an hour. | The narrator (Holmes) hails a cab and instructs the driver to follow the landau to the Church of St. Monica with similar urgency, also offering a half sovereign. | The narrator reflects on the implications of the relationship between the gentleman and the woman (friend or mistress) for the investigation, considering whether to focus on Briony Lodge or the gentleman's chambers.

scenes.title: Arrival at Briony Lodge and Staged Quarrel
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson leave Baker Street, arrive at Serpentine Avenue at dusk, and observe the lively street scene in front of Briony Lodge while waiting for its occupant. | Holmes, the King, and Watson enter the ransacked drawing-room of Briony Lodge, where Holmes discovers a photograph of Irene Adler and a letter addressed to him. | The King expresses his concerns about Irene Adler to Holmes and Watson while they are in a brougham, leading up to their arrival at Serpentine Avenue and Briony Lodge. | The lady's carriage arrives at Briony Lodge, and a pre-arranged quarrel breaks out among several men as she steps out, creating a diversion. | Watson arrives at Baker Street at the appointed time, but Holmes is not present, as informed by the landlady.

scenes.title: Instructions for Briony Lodge
scenes.description: Holmes gives Watson specific instructions for their arrival at Briony Lodge to intercept Miss Irene, emphasizing Watson's role as a neutral observer during the event. | The narrator arrives at Baker Street to meet Holmes, but finds him absent. The landlady informs him Holmes left early. The narrator waits by the fire, reflecting on Holmes's methods and the intriguing nature of his current case.

scenes.title: Recounting Briony Lodge Reconnaissance
scenes.description: Holmes describes to the narrator his morning's work, including his disguise as a groom and his detailed examination of Briony Lodge and its surroundings. | Holmes details to the Doctor how he orchestrated a disturbance, feigned injury with red paint, and used a simulated fire alarm to gain entry into the woman's house and discover the photograph's location. | The narrator is suddenly dragged to the altar of a church by Godfrey Norton to act as a witness for his marriage to Irene Adler, due to an informality in their license.

scenes.title: Information Gathering at the Mews
scenes.description: Holmes recounts how he assisted ostlers in a mews near Briony Lodge, receiving payment and refreshments in exchange for his help and gathering information. | The narrator arrives at the Church of St. Monica, finding the woman, the coachman, and a clergyman. Godfrey Norton then urgently approaches the narrator, asking for his help as a witness for a wedding.

scenes.title: Information Gathering at Serpentine-mews
scenes.description: Holmes, disguised, assists ostlers and cabmen at Serpentine-mews to gather detailed information about Miss Adler's habits and her male visitor, Mr. Godfrey Norton.

scenes.title: Contemplation near Briony Lodge
scenes.description: After gathering information, Holmes walks near Briony Lodge, reflecting on the significance of Mr. Godfrey Norton's role and his relationship with Miss Adler in the context of the case.

scenes.title: Arrival of the Gentleman at Briony Lodge
scenes.description: A handsome, moustached gentleman arrives at Briony Lodge in a hansom cab, appearing hurried, and brushes past the maid into the house.

scenes.title: Planning the Evening's Operation
scenes.description: Holmes discusses the upcoming operation with Watson, asking for his cooperation and outlining initial steps while eating a simple meal brought by Mrs. Turner.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains the Diversion Plan
scenes.description: Holmes instructs a confederate on how to create a diversion by throwing a smoke-rocket into a sitting-room window and raising a cry of fire.

scenes.title: Holmes's Reasoning on the Object's Location
scenes.description: Holmes explains his deduction that the lady keeps the significant object in her own house, despite past burglary attempts, because she would not trust it to others and needs it readily accessible. | While pacing in front of Briony Lodge, Holmes discusses how the impending marriage makes the photograph a 'double-edged weapon' and deduces that the woman does not carry the cabinet-sized photograph on her person.

scenes.title: Street Scuffle and Holmes' Injury
scenes.description: A scuffle breaks out between guardsmen, loungers, and a scissors-grinder. Holmes intervenes to protect a lady and is struck, falling to the ground with a bleeding face.

scenes.title: Holmes Brought into Briony Lodge
scenes.description: Holmes is slowly and solemnly carried into Briony Lodge and laid out in the principal room, observed by the narrator.

scenes.title: The 'Fire!' Alarm
scenes.description: Holmes signals Watson, who throws a smoke-rocket into the room, shouting 'Fire!'. The crowd panics, and smoke fills the room.

scenes.title: Walking Away from the Uproar
scenes.description: Holmes and the Doctor walk away from the scene of the uproar towards Edgeware Road, with Holmes expressing satisfaction with his plan.

scenes.title: Holmes recounts the fire alarm ruse
scenes.description: Holmes describes how he staged a fire alarm at the woman's house to discover the hiding place of the photograph, observing her reaction.

scenes.title: Planning the photograph's retrieval
scenes.description: Holmes and the narrator discuss the next steps to retrieve the photograph, planning to call with the King the following morning.

scenes.title: Journey to Briony Lodge and Discussion of Irene's Marriage
scenes.description: Holmes, the narrator, and the King depart Baker Street in the King's brougham, continuing their discussion about Irene Adler's marriage and its implications for the King's plan.

scenes.title: Encounter with the Servant
scenes.description: Holmes, the King, and Watson are met by an elderly woman at Briony Lodge who informs them that Irene Adler has left England with her husband.

scenes.title: Holmes Concludes His Meeting with the King and Narrator's Reflection
scenes.description: Holmes concludes his interaction with the King, requesting Irene's photograph, and then departs. The narrator reflects on how Holmes's plans were thwarted by Irene Adler's wit and Holmes's subsequent respect for her.

events.name: Discussion of Photograph's Strategic Value
events.description: A landau arrives shortly after the gentleman's departure, with its coachman in disarray. | A mysterious visitor, identifying as Count Von Kramm, arrives at Holmes's residence to discuss a sensitive matter, wearing a mask. | A note is received, instructing the recipient to be in their chamber at a certain hour for a visitor who may wear a mask, prompting Holmes and Watson to analyze it. | During the fire alarm ruse, the woman rushes to a recess behind a sliding panel, revealing the photograph's hiding spot. | Holmes changes his costume, showcasing his acting ability and adaptability for his role. | Holmes considers the possible relationships between Miss Adler and Mr. Godfrey Norton (client, friend, or mistress) and how this affects the location of the photograph and his investigative strategy. | Holmes discovers that Mr. Godfrey Norton is a lawyer from the Inner Temple, which he considers an ominous detail. | Holmes explains that the woman's impending marriage makes the compromising photograph a 'double-edged weapon'. | Holmes goes into his bedroom and emerges five minutes later, dressed in respectable tweed, shedding his disguise. | Holmes meticulously analyzes the paper of the mysterious note, using its texture, cost, and watermarks ('Eg', 'P', 'Gt') to deduce that it is German paper from Egria in Bohemia. | Holmes stages a fake fire alarm at the woman's house to observe her reaction and discover the hiding place of the photograph. | Holmes used the simulated fire alarm to make the woman instinctively reveal the hiding place of the photograph. | Irene Adler declares her intention to keep the photograph as a safeguard against the King, stating she loves a better man. | Irene Adler describes how she recognized Holmes's disguise and saw through his ruse during the 'fire alarm' incident. | Irene Adler leaves England with her husband by train from Charing Cross for the Continent. | Irene Adler recounts her disguise, following Holmes, and her subsequent flight with her husband to the Temple and out of the country. | Mr. Sherlock Holmes's best plans are beaten by Irene Adler's wit, leading to a great scandal threatening Bohemia. | Mr. Sherlock Holmes, the King of Bohemia, and a third person read Irene Norton's letter, which resolves the case of the compromising photograph. | Sherlock Holmes informs the King of Bohemia that Irene Adler married an English lawyer named Norton the previous day. | The King is about to marry Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, which makes the photograph a serious threat. | The King recounts five unsuccessful attempts to retrieve the photograph, including burglaries, luggage diversion, and waylaying. | The King's past affair with Irene Adler, which resulted in a compromising photograph. | The discovery at the Church of St. Monica that a wedding ceremony is about to take place, with Godfrey Norton urgently seeking a witness. | The gentleman leaves Briony Lodge in a hansom cab, instructing the driver to rush to specific locations. | The narrator's marriage caused him and Holmes to drift apart, explaining the narrator's recent absence. | The public proclamation of the King's betrothal is scheduled for next Monday, the day Irene Adler plans to send the photograph. | The visitor reveals that the matter concerns a potential immense scandal that could compromise the House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia, and requests absolute secrecy from Holmes and Watson.

events.name: Narrator's return to civil practice
events.description: The narrator mentions having returned to civil medical practice.

events.name: Narrator's return to Baker Street
events.description: On March 20, 1888, the narrator's path leads him through Baker Street, prompting a desire to see Holmes.

events.name: Watson visits Holmes
events.description: Driven by a desire to see Holmes and his extraordinary powers in action, Watson visits his friend's rooms.

events.name: Holmes deduces Watson's recent life
events.description: Upon Watson's arrival, Holmes makes several observations and deductions about Watson's marriage, weight gain, return to practice, recent exposure to wet weather, and the clumsiness of his servant.

events.name: Holmes explains observation vs. seeing
events.description: Holmes uses the example of the steps to illustrate the difference between passive seeing and active observation.

events.name: Holmes receives a mysterious note
events.description: Holmes receives an anonymous, undated note announcing an important consultation.

events.name: A gentleman announces his visit
events.description: The note details that a gentleman will call upon Holmes at a quarter to eight for a consultation on a matter of 'deepest moment'.

events.name: Arrival of the client
events.description: The sound of horses' hoofs, grating wheels, a bell pull, and a heavy step indicate the arrival of Holmes's client.

events.name: Arrival of the tall, masked man
events.description: A very tall, richly dressed man, wearing a black vizard mask and speaking with a German accent, arrives at Holmes's residence.

events.name: King of Bohemia reveals his identity
events.description: The agitated visitor tears off his mask and declares himself to be the King of Bohemia, Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein.

events.name: King of Bohemia explains his incognito visit
events.description: The King explains that the matter is so delicate he could not confide it to an agent, leading him to come incognito from Prague to consult Holmes personally.

events.name: King of Bohemia begins recounting past acquaintance
events.description: The King begins to explain the facts of his case, starting with his acquaintance with a well-known adventuress during a visit to Warsaw five years prior.

events.name: The King reveals his entanglement with Irene Adler
events.description: Your Majesty informs Holmes about his past relationship with Irene Adler, the existence of compromising letters, and his fear of blackmail.

events.name: Holmes learns about Irene Adler's background
events.description: Holmes, through his index, quickly retrieves information about Irene Adler's birth, career as a contralto and prima donna, and current residence.

events.name: Threat to Send Photograph
events.description: Irene Adler threatens to send the compromising photograph to the family of the King's fiancée. | The rapid journey of the woman in a landau and the narrator in a cab to the Church of St. Monica for an urgent, unspecified event.

events.name: King reveals photograph sending date
events.description: The King informs Holmes that the photograph will be sent on the upcoming Monday.

events.name: King provides payment
events.description: The King gives Holmes three hundred pounds in gold and seven hundred in notes for expenses.

events.name: King provides Mademoiselle's address
events.description: The King gives Holmes the address of Briony Lodge, Serpentine Avenue, St. John’s Wood.

events.name: King departs
events.description: The King leaves Holmes's residence in his royal brougham.

events.name: Watson arrives at Baker Street
events.description: Watson arrives at Baker Street at three o'clock, as requested by Holmes, but finds him absent.

events.name: Gentleman's Arrival at Briony Lodge
events.description: A gentleman arrives in a hansom cab at Briony Lodge, showing signs of urgency. | Holmes and Watson arrive at Serpentine Avenue, outside Briony Lodge, at dusk. | The narrator arrives at Baker Street at three o'clock to meet Holmes, but he is not present.

events.name: Holmes Returns in Disguise
events.description: Holmes returns to his residence disguised as a drunken-looking groom, surprising the narrator.

events.name: Holmes's Disguise as a Groom
events.description: Holmes adopted the character of a groom out of work to facilitate his investigation of Miss Irene Adler, leveraging the camaraderie among 'horsey men'.

events.name: Reconnaissance of Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes thoroughly examined the exterior and accessible points of Briony Lodge, noting its structure, security features like the Chubb lock, and easily opened window fasteners. | Holmes, the King, and Watson find the drawing-room at Briony Lodge ransacked, indicating a hurried departure or search. | The King of Bohemia rushes into Holmes's rooms, impatient for news regarding Irene Adler.

events.name: Information Gathering from Ostlers
events.description: Holmes engaged with stable workers (ostlers) in a nearby mews, offering assistance and receiving small payments and refreshments, which aided his intelligence gathering.

events.name: Holmes Gathers Information on Miss Adler and Godfrey Norton
events.description: Holmes, disguised, obtains detailed information from ostlers and cabmen at Serpentine-mews regarding Miss Adler's daily routine and her frequent male visitor, Mr. Godfrey Norton.

events.name: Narrator's Deliberation on Investigation Focus
events.description: Holmes deduces that the woman does not carry the cabinet-sized photograph on her person, citing its size and previous attempts to retrieve it. | The narrator ponders whether to continue work at Briony Lodge or shift attention to the gentleman's chambers, depending on the nature of the relationship between the gentleman and the woman.

events.name: Narrator becomes wedding witness
events.description: The narrator is unexpectedly pressed into service as a witness for the marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton.

events.name: Holmes's Staged Uproar and Feigned Injury
events.description: Holmes orchestrated a disturbance in the street and pretended to be injured to be carried into the woman's house. | Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton are married in a church, with the narrator as an impromptu witness.

events.name: Irene Adler gives a sovereign
events.description: Irene Adler gives the narrator a sovereign coin as a memento of the wedding.

events.name: Couple separates after wedding
events.description: Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton separate at the church door, going their own ways after their marriage.

events.name: Irene Adler's plan to drive in the park
events.description: Irene Adler informs the narrator that she will drive in the park at five as usual.

events.name: Holmes requests Watson's cooperation
events.description: Holmes asks Watson for his help in an operation that might involve breaking the law and risk of arrest, which Watson readily agrees to.

events.name: Holmes outlines the plan for Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes explains to Watson that they must be at Briony Lodge by seven to meet Miss Irene upon her return, and instructs Watson on his specific role during the operation, including not interfering.

events.name: Holmes explains the smoke-rocket ruse
events.description: Holmes details a plan to a confederate involving throwing a smoke-rocket into a window and raising a cry of fire to create a diversion.

events.name: Holmes disguises himself as a clergyman
events.description: Holmes changes his attire and demeanor to assume the character of a Nonconformist clergyman for an upcoming task.

events.name: Arrival of the lady's carriage
events.description: The lady's smart little landau arrives at the door of Briony Lodge.

events.name: Staged quarrel outside Briony Lodge
events.description: A fierce quarrel erupts among loafers, guardsmen, and a scissors-grinder as the lady exits her carriage, part of Holmes's plan.

events.name: Scuffle in the street
events.description: A fight erupts between several men, including guardsmen, loungers, and a scissors-grinder.

events.name: Holmes is injured
events.description: Holmes is struck during the scuffle while protecting a lady and falls to the ground, bleeding.

events.name: Irene Adler allows Holmes entry
events.description: Irene Adler gives permission for the injured Holmes to be brought into her home, Briony Lodge.

events.name: Holmes is carried into Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes is transported into the principal room of Briony Lodge after his injury.

events.name: Holmes feigns injury
events.description: Holmes is borne into Briony Lodge, pretending to be injured, as part of a plan to observe Irene Adler's reaction and locate a hidden item.

events.name: Watson throws smoke-rocket
events.description: Upon Holmes's signal, Watson throws a smoke-rocket into the room, shouting 'Fire!' to create a diversion and panic.

events.name: Crowd reacts to 'fire'
events.description: A crowd of spectators, including gentlemen, ostlers, and servant maids, shrieks 'Fire!' as thick clouds of smoke fill the room.

events.name: Holmes declares false alarm
events.description: Holmes's voice is heard from within, assuring everyone that the alarm is false after the ruse has served its purpose.

events.name: Watson and Holmes reunite
events.description: Watson escapes the chaotic scene and meets Holmes at the corner of the street, leaving the scene of uproar.

events.name: Plan to Retrieve the Photograph
events.description: Holmes outlines his plan to visit the house with the King the next morning at eight o'clock to retrieve the photograph.

events.name: Mysterious Greeting on Baker Street
events.description: A slim youth in an ulster greets Sherlock Holmes by name on Baker Street, prompting Holmes to wonder about his identity.

events.name: Discovery of Photograph and Letter
events.description: Holmes finds a hidden photograph of Irene Adler and a letter addressed to him within the ransacked room.

events.name: Irene Adler's Letter is Read
events.description: Sherlock Holmes, Watson, and the King read Irene Adler's letter, which details her successful evasion and departure.

events.name: Holmes requests Irene's photograph
events.description: Instead of a monetary reward, Mr. Sherlock Holmes asks the King of Bohemia for Irene Norton's photograph, which the King grants.

crimes.name: The Singular Narrative of Mr. Jabez Wilson
crimes.description: A mysterious 'prank' or scheme involving the Red-Headed League, designed to deceive Mr. Wilson and costing the perpetrators money, with an unknown ultimate object. | A puzzling case brought by Mr. Wilson that Holmes considers a 'three pipe problem'. | Criminals are planning to steal 30,000 napoleons from the bank's cellar. | Jabez Wilson suspects the Red-Headed League job is a great hoax or fraud due to its unusual nature and high pay for simple work, though he cannot imagine its object. | The central mystery involving Mr. Wilson and the Red-headed League. | The extraordinary story of the red-headed copier of the Encyclopædia and the impending nocturnal expedition, which Watson finds confusing. | The unusual and suspicious nature of the advertisement for the Red-Headed League, offering a high salary for nominal services to red-headed men. | The central mystery of the 'singular story' involving a fraudulent scheme related to the Red-Headed League, which Holmes is investigating. | The scheme involving the Red-Headed League, which resulted in Mr. Wilson losing his job and income, and the disappearance of the individuals involved. | The sudden and unexplained dissolution of The Red-Headed League, leading to the client's loss of employment and the disappearance of its organizers. | The suspicious and unusual process of applying for and being accepted into the Red-Headed League, hinting at an underlying scheme. | The type of perplexing problems brought by red-headed clients, referring to the central scheme of the Red-Headed League. | The unknown nature of Mr. Jabez Wilson's case, which is described as singular and potentially criminal, but its exact nature is yet to be determined. | The unusual advertisement for a vacancy in the League of the Red-headed Men, which promises a fortune for red-headed individuals.

crimes.name: Termination of Red-Headed League employment
crimes.description: The narrator's lucrative employment with the Red-Headed League abruptly ended without warning, and the office was found locked.

crimes.name: Contemplated Crime at Coburg Square
crimes.description: A serious crime that is currently 'in contemplation' at Coburg Square, which Holmes intends to stop.

crimes.name: Attempted Theft of £30,000
crimes.description: The crime for which John Clay is being pursued, involving a significant sum of money.

crimes.name: John Clay's Attempted Bank Robbery
crimes.description: John Clay's criminal activity, referred to as 'cracking a crib', which Mr. Merryweather, a bank director, is personally interested in stopping.

crimes.name: Attempted Bank Robbery
crimes.description: A determined attempt at bank robbery that was detected and defeated by Holmes. | Criminals are attempting to break into a bank vault by coming up through the floor. | Criminals are tunneling from a cellar to the City and Suburban Bank to steal bullion, and are expected to make their attempt tonight. | The criminals are about to break into the vault to commit a robbery. | The impending attempt to rob the bank vault by tunneling from an adjacent property. | The intruders, John Clay and Archie, are caught emerging from a hole, presumably after attempting to rob a bank, as indicated by the mention of 'chisel and bags' and the 'red-headed idea'.

crimes.name: Planned Theft via Tunneling
crimes.description: A scheme to get a pawnbroker out of his shop daily, allowing an accomplice to dig a tunnel from the cellar to another building for a large-scale theft.

objects.name: dirty and wrinkled newspaper

objects.name: arc-and-compass breastpin

objects.name: right cuff
objects.description: Mr. Jabez Wilson's right cuff, shiny for five inches, indicating recent writing.

objects.name: left one
objects.description: Mr. Jabez Wilson's left cuff, with a smooth patch near the elbow, indicating where it rests on a desk while writing.

objects.name: fish that you have tattooed
objects.description: A tattoo of a fish with delicate pink scales on Mr. Jabez Wilson's right wrist, peculiar to China.

objects.name: Chinese coin
objects.description: A coin hanging from Mr. Jabez Wilson, further indicating his connection to China. | A coin hanging from Mr. Wilson's watch-chain, used by Holmes as a clue to deduce Mr. Wilson's connection to China.

objects.name: fishes’ scales
objects.description: Mentioned by Holmes as being stained pink, a practice peculiar to China, used in a deduction about Mr. Wilson.

objects.name: watch-chain
objects.description: The chain from which Mr. Wilson's Chinese coin hangs.

objects.name: advertisement
objects.description: A printed notice that announces a vacancy in the League of the Red-headed Men and provides an address for particulars. | The advertisement for the Red-Headed League, used to lure the pawnbroker into the scheme. | The advertisement that had a significant effect on Mr. Wilson's fortunes. | The printed notice from 'The Red-Headed League' that details the vacancy and requirements, initiating the central mystery.

objects.name: _Encyclopædia Britannica_
objects.description: A newspaper from April 27, 1890, in which the significant advertisement appeared. | The object being copied as part of the scheme to get the pawnbroker out of the way. | The supposed work the pawnbroker was hired to copy, used as a pretext to ensure his daily absence. | The set of books from which Mr. Jabez Wilson is required to copy text for the Red-Headed League.

objects.name: camera
objects.description: An object used by Vincent Spaulding for his photography hobby. | Used by Spaulding for photography.

objects.name: paper
objects.description: The newspaper containing the advertisement for the Red-Headed League, brought by Spaulding.

objects.name: snuff
objects.description: A huge pinch of snuff used by Holmes's client to refresh his memory.

objects.name: hair
objects.description: Mr. Wilson's red hair, which is a key requirement for the Red-Headed League and is physically tested for authenticity.

objects.name: fund
objects.description: The financial endowment left by a noble benefactor for the propagation and maintenance of red-heads, which the Red-Headed League manages.

objects.name: wigs
objects.description: Mentioned by Mr. Duncan Ross as a past means of deception used by applicants.

objects.name: paint
objects.description: Mentioned by Mr. Duncan Ross as a past means of deception used by applicants.

objects.name: cobbler's wax
objects.description: Mentioned by Mr. Duncan Ross as a past means of deception used by applicants.

objects.description: Ink bought by Jabez Wilson for his copying work for the Red-Headed League.

objects.description: A pen bought by Jabez Wilson for his copying work for the Red-Headed League.

objects.name: a little square of cardboard
objects.description: A notice hammered onto the office door, announcing the end of the Red-Headed League. | A piece of white cardboard hammered onto a door, announcing 'THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890.'

objects.description: The same notice, held up by the narrator for Mr. Holmes to read.

objects.name: black clay pipe

objects.name: gilt balls

objects.name: brown board with JABEZ WILSON
objects.description: A sign on the corner house indicating the pawnbroker's business and its owner.

objects.description: Used by Holmes to beat upon the pavement to ascertain the cellar's extent. | Used by Holmes to thump vigorously upon the pavement, possibly as part of his observation or a habit. | Used by Mr. Merryweather to strike the vault floor, revealing its hollowness.
