crimes.name: Imprisonment and Impersonation of Miss Alice Rucastle
crimes.description: A situation involving an unusual salary, curious conditions, and light duties, pointing to something abnormal, which prompts an urgent summons from HUNTER. | A situation offered to Mr. Holmes for consultation, marking his 'zero-point' for a new case. | An unusually high-paying job offer with strange conditions, prompting Miss Hunter to consult Holmes. | Miss Alice Rucastle is being held captive, and Miss Hunter has been hired to impersonate her to deceive others, particularly her fiancé. | Miss Hunter's inability to understand the reasons for the Rucastles' conduct, which makes her uneasy. | Mr. Rucastle imprisoned his daughter, Miss Alice, and coerced her to sign away her inheritance, leading to her illness and subsequent confinement. | Mrs. Toller states she was unable to leave the cellar, implying she was held against her will. | The central mystery concerning the 'poor girl' who is in the power of the household, potentially endangered by the cruel child and cunning man. | The central mystery surrounding a suite of rooms that the narrator is forbidden to enter, prompting her to investigate out of a sense of duty. | The client's employment under unusual conditions, including an abnormal salary, curious conditions, and light duties, which Holmes suspects may lead to danger or be part of a plot. | The mystery surrounding a heavily barricaded and locked room, from which steps and a shadow are observed, causing the narrator intense terror. | The mystery surrounding a locked suite of rooms with shuttered windows, and Mr. Rucastle's suspicious behavior regarding it. | The overarching mystery surrounding the sinister house, Miss Hunter's employment, and Miss Rucastle's confinement and escape. | The peculiar and unexplained demands made by the Rucastles for Miss Hunter to read aloud, stop abruptly, change her dress, and their efforts to prevent her from looking out the window. | The prisoner, previously confined in the room, has either escaped or been carried off by someone. | The unusual and unsettling conditions of the narrator's employment, involving forced laughter and reading aloud. | Violet Hunter is anxious about accepting a governess situation due to a 'very strange experience' and seeks Holmes's advice.
crimes.motive: To prevent Miss Alice Rucastle from communicating with her fiancé and to control her inheritance or relationships.

objects.description: A chain heard rattling, restraining Carlo the mastiff.

objects.name: a great coil
objects.description: A coil of the narrator's cut hair, stored at the bottom of her trunk.

objects.name: my trunk
objects.description: A trunk where the narrator stored her cut hair. | The narrator's luggage, from which she retrieves her own hair for comparison.

objects.name: chest of drawers
objects.description: An old piece of furniture in the narrator's room, with a locked lower drawer that she cannot access.

objects.name: drawer
objects.description: A locked drawer in the narrator's room, which she opens to find a mysterious coil of hair.

objects.name: bunch of keys
objects.description: Used by the narrator to open the locked drawer in her room.

objects.name: my coil of hair
objects.description: A coil of hair found in the locked drawer, which is identical in tint and thickness to the narrator's own hair.

objects.name: keys
objects.description: Duplicates of Mr. Rucastle’s keys, provided by Miss Hunter to Holmes. | Held by Mr. Rucastle when he was seen coming out of a locked door in the uninhabited wing. | Mr. Rucastle's keys, used to lock the mysterious suite door.

objects.name: large black linen bag
objects.description: An object seen being carried by Toller through the door of the deserted rooms, suggesting something is being transported or concealed.

objects.name: the key
objects.description: A key to lock Mrs. Toller in the cellar. | Left in the door of the forbidden rooms by a drunken Toller, providing the narrator with an opportunity to enter. | The missing key for the locked barricaded door.

objects.name: broad bars of an iron bed
objects.description: Used to barricade the centre door from the outside.

objects.name: padlock
objects.description: Used to secure one end of the iron bar to a ring in the wall.

objects.name: stout cord
objects.description: Used to fasten the other end of the iron bar.

objects.name: dog
objects.description: A huge, famished brute, intentionally loosed, which attacks Rucastle and is subsequently shot. | A savage creature in the household, feared by Miss Hunter, over whom Toller has influence. | An animal let loose at night to prevent communication. | An unfed, dangerous animal deliberately loosed to attack.

objects.name: lock
objects.description: A good strong lock on the wine-cellar, inquired about by Holmes.

objects.name: her tresses
objects.description: The cut hair of Miss Alice Rucastle, found by Miss Hunter, indicating her hair was cut short.

objects.name: the girl’s dress
objects.description: A dress worn by Miss Hunter to impersonate Miss Alice Rucastle.

objects.name: barricade
objects.description: An obstruction blocking the door to the prisoner's room, described by Miss Hunter.

objects.name: cord
objects.description: Part of the barricade, cut by Holmes.

objects.name: transverse bar
objects.description: Part of the barricade, removed by Holmes.

objects.name: door
objects.description: An old, rickety door to the prisoner's room that was forced open.

objects.name: pallet bed
objects.description: One of the few items of furniture found in the empty prisoner's room.

objects.name: small table
objects.description: One of the few items of furniture found in the empty prisoner's room.

objects.name: basketful of linen
objects.description: One of the few items found in the empty prisoner's room.

objects.name: skylight
objects.description: A window on the roof, used as an entry/exit point by an unknown person. | An open window above the room, identified as the escape route.

objects.name: ladder
objects.description: A long light ladder found against the eaves, used by the prisoner to escape through the skylight. | An object made ready to facilitate an escape from the house.

objects.name: long light ladder
objects.description: A ladder found against the eaves, used to access the skylight.

objects.name: pistol
objects.description: Watson's firearm, kept ready for a potential confrontation.

objects.name: heavy stick
objects.description: A weapon carried by the fat man during the confrontation.

objects.name: revolver
objects.description: Watson's firearm, mentioned as being ready.

objects.name: gun
objects.description: Used by the narrator to shoot the attacking dog, saving Rucastle's life.

objects.name: paper
objects.description: A document Mr. Rucastle wanted Miss Alice to sign to give him control over her money.

deductions.observation: It is half-past ten now. (The appointed time for Violet Hunter's visit) and a ring is heard at the door.
deductions.inference: The timing of the ring coincides with Violet Hunter's scheduled appointment.
deductions.conclusion: The person at the door is Violet Hunter.

deductions.observation: They offer £ 120 a year, when they could have their pick for £ 40.
deductions.inference: There must be some strong reason behind this discrepancy.

deductions.observation: scattered houses and their isolation in the countryside
deductions.inference: This isolation provides impunity with which crime may be committed there.
deductions.conclusion: Such places always fill me with a certain horror, as they are less safe than the lowest and vilest alleys in London.

deductions.observation: The lowest and vilest alleys in London do not present a more dreadful record of sin than does the smiling and beautiful countryside.
deductions.inference: Public opinion and the machinery of justice in towns deter crime, whereas in lonely country houses with ignorant folk, hidden wickedness can go unnoticed.
deductions.conclusion: The five miles of country around isolated homes can make them dangerous places for hidden crimes.

deductions.observation: If this lady who appeals to us for help had gone to live in Winchester, I should never have had a fear for her. It is the five miles of country which makes the danger.
deductions.inference: The danger is associated with the isolated rural setting, not an immediate personal threat that would prevent her from traveling.
deductions.conclusion: She is not personally threatened (in a way that restricts her movement).

deductions.observation: If she can come to Winchester to meet us she can get away.
deductions.inference: Her ability to travel freely to Winchester indicates she is not being held captive or physically restrained.
deductions.conclusion: She has her freedom.

deductions.observation: Miss Hunter was brought to Copper Beeches, made to cut her hair, and wear specific clothes.
deductions.inference: She was brought there to personate someone.
deductions.conclusion: The real person is imprisoned in this chamber.

deductions.observation: Miss Alice Rucastle was said to have gone to America. Miss Hunter resembles her in height, figure, and hair color. Miss Hunter found cut tresses.
deductions.inference: The prisoner is Miss Alice Rucastle, whose hair was cut off, possibly due to illness, and Miss Hunter's hair had to be sacrificed to match.
deductions.conclusion: Miss Alice Rucastle is the imprisoned person, and Miss Hunter is impersonating her.

deductions.observation: A man in the road (possibly Miss Alice Rucastle's fiancé) saw Miss Hunter (dressed as Miss Rucastle) laughing and gesturing. The dog is let loose at night.
deductions.inference: The man was convinced Miss Rucastle was happy and no longer desired his attentions. The dog prevents him from communicating with her.
deductions.conclusion: The Rucastles are actively deceiving Miss Alice Rucastle's fiancé and preventing contact.

deductions.observation: This child’s disposition is abnormally cruel, merely for cruelty’s sake
deductions.inference: whether he derives this from his smiling father, as I should suspect, or from his mother
deductions.conclusion: it bodes evil for the poor girl who is in their power.

deductions.observation: The prisoner's room is empty, the skylight above was open, and a long light ladder is found against the eaves.
deductions.inference: The prisoner escaped through the skylight.
deductions.conclusion: The ladder was used to facilitate the escape from the skylight.

deductions.observation: here’s the end of a long light ladder against the eaves.
deductions.inference: The ladder was used to reach the skylight.
deductions.conclusion: That is how he did it (entered/exited via the skylight).

deductions.observation: step I hear now upon the stair.
deductions.inference: The steps belong to the clever and dangerous man who used the ladder.
deductions.conclusion: It would be wise for Watson to have his pistol ready for a confrontation.

deductions.observation: Mrs. Toller's statement to Miss Hunter: 'Ah, miss, it is a pity you didn’t let me know what you were planning, for I would have told you that your pains were wasted.'
deductions.inference: Her statement implies prior knowledge of Miss Hunter's plans and the futility of those plans, suggesting she has intimate knowledge of the situation at the house.
deductions.conclusion: Mrs. Toller knows more about this matter than anyone else.

deductions.observation: The speaker's account of Miss Alice's unhappiness, her father's attempts to control her money, and her subsequent illness.
deductions.inference: The information provided makes the matter fairly clear, allowing for further deductions.
deductions.conclusion: Mr. Rucastle took to a system of imprisonment.

deductions.observation: Mr. Rucastle's system of imprisonment and the need to get rid of Mr. Fowler.
deductions.inference: Mr. Rucastle would need to remove Mr. Fowler as an obstacle to his plans.
deductions.conclusion: Mr. Rucastle brought Miss Hunter down from London in order to get rid of the disagreeable persistence of Mr. Fowler.

deductions.observation: Mr. Fowler being described as a 'persevering man' and a 'good seaman'.
deductions.inference: A persevering man, especially a seaman, would not easily give up on his objective.
deductions.conclusion: Mr. Fowler blockaded the house.

deductions.observation: Miss Hunter was brought from London to get rid of Mr. Fowler's persistence. Mr. Fowler, a persevering man, blockaded the house and convinced Mrs. Toller with 'certain arguments, metallic or otherwise'. Mrs. Toller ensured her husband had drink and a ladder was ready when the master left.
deductions.inference: Mr. Fowler successfully enlisted Mrs. Toller's help, likely through bribery or persuasion, to facilitate Miss Rucastle's escape. Mrs. Toller's actions, such as providing drink to her husband and preparing a ladder, were instrumental in the plan.
deductions.conclusion: Mrs. Toller was an accomplice in Mr. Fowler's plan to help Miss Rucastle escape from the Rucastle household.

scenes.title: Discussion on Case Records and Storytelling
scenes.description: Sherlock Holmes and Watson engage in a philosophical discussion about the nature of art, the recording of their cases, and the balance between sensationalism and logical reasoning in Watson's narratives.

scenes.title: Discussion of Violet Hunter's Letter and Anticipation of Her Arrival
scenes.description: A character explains the history of Miss Alice's mistreatment by her father, Mr. Rucastle, concerning her inheritance and her relationship with Mr. Fowler. Holmes then makes several deductions based on this information. | After the client leaves, Holmes predicts they will hear from her soon. A fortnight passes, and the narrator reflects on the strange circumstances of her employment. | Holmes and Watson arrive at the house, greeted by Miss Hunter, who provides keys and information about Mrs. Toller and her husband. | Holmes and Watson force open the rickety door and rush into the room, only to find it empty, save for a few sparse items. They realize the prisoner is gone and the skylight is open. | Holmes and the narrator discuss a letter from Violet Hunter regarding a governess position and anticipate her arrival at half-past ten. | Holmes and the narrator discuss the nature of Holmes's past cases, the public's perception, and the current decline in interesting cases, culminating in Holmes receiving and presenting a letter about a new situation. | Holmes and the narrator listen to Miss Hunter's story. Holmes then paces and begins to question Miss Hunter about Toller's state, the Rucastles' plans, and the presence of a cellar. | Holmes deduces the prisoner escaped through the skylight and climbs onto the roof, where he discovers a long light ladder, confirming the method of escape. | Holmes encourages Miss Hunter to continue her narrative, finding it interesting. | Holmes explains his deduction about the child's cruel disposition and its implications for the 'poor girl' to Watson and their client, who then urges immediate action. | Holmes summarizes the events to Mrs. Toller, who confirms them, and then prepares to leave with Watson and Miss Hunter as the country surgeon and Mrs. Rucastle arrive. | Holmes, Watson, and Miss Hunter are on the roof/in a room, examining a skylight and discovering a ladder used for entry/exit. | Holmes, Watson, and Miss Hunter pursue the fat man down the stairs, hear a dog attack, and rush outside to find an elderly man in distress. | Inside the drawing-room, while attending to Rucastle, Mrs. Toller enters and reveals she has crucial information, implying she was confined in the cellar. | Late one night, an urgent telegram arrives from HUNTER, interrupting Holmes's chemical researches and summoning him to Winchester. | Miss Hunter describes the unpleasant appearance and conduct of the servants, Toller and his wife, noting Toller's drunkenness and Mr. Rucastle's indifference. She mentions spending most of her time in the nursery and her own room. | Miss Hunter explains her ability to come to Winchester, her need to return before three o'clock to look after the child, and asks Holmes for advice. | Miss Hunter is reading aloud when she is suddenly ordered to cease and change her dress, sparking her intense curiosity about the Rucastles' 'extraordinary performance'. | Miss Hunter recounts making up her mind, sending a wire from the office, and her return home, feeling easier but then fearing the dog. | Miss Hunter uses her makeshift mirror to observe a small bearded man in Southampton Road, but Mrs. Rucastle notices her trick and, along with Jephro, questions Miss Hunter about the man. | On a cold spring morning, after breakfast, in their Baker Street room, Sherlock Holmes, having been silent while reading advertisements, begins to lecture Watson on his literary style, emphasizing logic over sensationalism. | The client describes Westaway’s, a governess agency in the West End, its founder Westaway, and its manager Miss Stoper. | The client expresses her anxiety about her new employment, Holmes reassures her of his help, and she decides to proceed to Hampshire, feeling much stronger. | The content of the letter from Jephro Rucastle, detailing the peculiar conditions of the governess position at The Copper Beeches, including salary, dress code, and hair requirements. | The fates of Mr. Rucastle, Mr. Fowler, Miss Rucastle, and Miss Hunter are revealed after the resolution of the case. | The narrator and Holmes discuss train times and postpone work in preparation for a journey to Winchester. | The narrator describes what she found immediately after slipping through the forbidden door: a bare passage leading to three doors, two of which opened into dusty, cheerless empty rooms. | The narrator explores empty rooms, finds a door barricaded with an iron bed bar, padlock, and cord, and discovers it's locked with a missing key. She observes light from beneath and hears steps and sees a shadow, leading to terror. | The narrator is interviewed by a gentleman for a governess position, where he expresses enthusiasm for her suitability and offers a surprisingly high salary of £100 a year, confirming it with a note from his pocket-book. | The narrator leaves the house to go to an office half a mile away to send a wire to Mr. Holmes. | The narrator observes the shuttered windows of the mysterious suite from the grounds, and Mr. Rucastle approaches, offering a suspicious explanation about a 'dark room' for photography. | The narrator recounts observing the layout of the house, noting an uninhabited wing with a locked door, and later encountering Mr. Rucastle emerging from that very door with keys in hand. | The narrator recounts to Mr. Holmes her strong desire to investigate a mysterious suite of rooms, her observation of Toller's activities, and how she seized an opportunity to enter when Toller left the key in the door. | Toller alerts Holmes and the narrator that the dog has been loosed. They rush out to find the dog attacking Rucastle. The narrator shoots the dog, and they carry the mangled Rucastle into the house. | Two days later, the strange ritual is repeated, with the addition of the narrator being asked to read aloud from a yellow-backed novel, which is abruptly stopped by Mr. Rucastle. | Violet Hunter arrives at Holmes's residence, introduces herself, and begins to explain her 'very strange experience' to Holmes and the narrator, seeking their advice.

scenes.title: Holmes prepares to listen
scenes.description: Holmes is favourably impressed by his new client and composes himself to listen to her story.

scenes.title: Client's past employment and job search
scenes.description: The client recounts her five years as a governess for Colonel Spence Munro, his relocation to Halifax, Nova Scotia, and her subsequent unsuccessful search for a new situation.

scenes.title: Encounter at Miss Stoper's office
scenes.description: The client describes her last visit to Westaway's, where she found Miss Stoper accompanied by a 'prodigiously stout man' who seemed very interested in the ladies entering.

scenes.title: Miss Hunter Presents Rucastle's Letter to Holmes
scenes.description: After two quiet days, Mrs. Rucastle whispers to her husband, who then asks Miss Hunter to wear a specific electric-blue dress, acknowledging her recently cut hair. | Holmes and the narrator consult a Bradshaw to find a suitable train to Winchester for the following day, with Holmes deciding to postpone his chemical analysis. | Holmes and the narrator travel by train through the Hampshire countryside, where Holmes reflects on the potential for crime in isolated rural areas. | Holmes, Watson, and Miss Hunter proceed to the barricaded door. Holmes attempts to unlock it with the provided keys, then cuts the cord and removes the bar, but the lock remains stubborn. They decide to force the door. | Miss Hunter recounts her decision to accept the unusual employment offer and reads the letter from Jephro Rucastle to Mr. Holmes. | On her first day at Copper Beeches, Mr. Rucastle shows Miss Hunter a chained mastiff named Carlo in an outhouse. | Terrified after the confrontation, the narrator retreats to her room and decides to seek advice from Mr. Holmes. | The narrator recounts to Mr. Holmes the details of a job offer she received, including the gentleman's strange customs and the location of the employment.

scenes.title: Job Interview with Unusual Conditions
scenes.description: A fat man appears at the door, confronts Holmes, Watson, and Miss Hunter, and is questioned by Holmes about his daughter before fleeing. | A young lady (the narrator) is interviewed for a governess position by a man who proposes several unusual conditions, including obeying his wife's commands, wearing a specific dress, and cutting her hair short. The narrator refuses the condition regarding her hair, leading to the termination of the interview. | The terrified narrator runs from the barricaded door and encounters Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting outside. He questions her about her fright, his manner appearing overly coaxing to her.

scenes.title: Encounter at the Locked Door
scenes.description: Miss Hunter refuses a job offer, much to the annoyance of Miss Stoper, the manageress. | The narrator ascends the stair and encounters Mr. Rucastle, who is coming out of a locked suite of rooms, looking angry and secretive, and locks the door.

scenes.title: Reconsideration at Lodgings
scenes.description: Holmes, Watson, and the client arrive at Copper Beeches at seven o'clock, where Miss Hunter is waiting on the door-step, and a loud thudding noise is heard from downstairs. | Miss Hunter, back at her lodgings, reconsiders her refusal due to financial difficulties, and then receives a letter.

scenes.title: Consultation about the Copper Beeches Offer
scenes.description: Miss Hunter discusses the suspicious employment letter from Jephro Rucastle with Mr. Holmes, seeking his advice on the peculiar job offer and its unusually high pay.

scenes.title: Holmes's Initial Assessment and Need for Data
scenes.description: The narrator reflects on the abnormal nature of the situation, while Holmes, despite his concern, expresses his inability to form conclusions without more data.

scenes.title: Holmes's Philosophy on Countryside Crime
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the nature of crime, with Holmes arguing that the countryside can harbor more dreadful hidden sins than urban alleys, due to lack of public oversight. They also discuss the safety of the lady who has appealed for help.

scenes.title: Arrival at The Black Swan and Meeting Miss Hunter
scenes.description: Holmes and (implied) Watson arrive at The Black Swan inn, where they meet Miss Hunter, who expresses her gratitude and need for their advice.

scenes.title: Miss Hunter Begins Her Account
scenes.description: Miss Hunter starts to recount her experiences, mentioning her promise to Mr. Rucastle and her initial observations and unease regarding the Rucastles' conduct and the Copper Beeches.

scenes.title: Description of Copper Beeches and Introduction to Rucastle Family
scenes.description: The narrator describes the house known as Copper Beeches, its surroundings, and is introduced to Mr. Rucastle's wife and child. The narrator also reflects on Mrs. Rucastle's character and learns about the departure of Mr. Rucastle's elder daughter to Philadelphia.

scenes.title: Description of the Rucastle family and servants
scenes.description: The narrator describes Mrs. Rucastle's character, her devotion to her family, and her hidden sorrow. He also details the unpleasant nature of her son and the rough appearance and conduct of the servant, Toller.

scenes.title: The Peculiar Dress and the Rucastles' Reaction
scenes.description: Miss Hunter describes the electric-blue dress, noting its peculiar shade, material, signs of prior wear, and perfect fit. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle express an exaggerated delight at her appearance in the dress in the drawing-room.

scenes.title: First Strange Ritual in the Drawing-Room
scenes.description: Miss Hunter recounts an incident where a man stared at her from the road, leading to Mrs. Rucastle's intervention and the drawing of the blind. | The narrator describes finding a locked drawer in her room, opening it with her keys, and discovering a coil of hair identical to her own, causing her great bewilderment. | The narrator is confronted by a man after exploring the empty wing of the house, leading to a verbal threat. | The narrator's initial experience with Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle in the drawing-room, where Mr. Rucastle tells funny stories and expects the narrator to laugh, while Mrs. Rucastle remains somber.

scenes.title: Devising a Means of Observation
scenes.description: Consumed by the desire to see what was being hidden, Miss Hunter devises a method using a piece of her broken hand-mirror concealed in her handkerchief.

scenes.title: Warning about the dog
scenes.description: old Toller warns the narrator about the dangerous dog that is let loose every night to guard the property.

scenes.title: Night observation of the giant dog
scenes.description: The narrator looks out her bedroom window at night and observes a giant, tawny-tinted dog crossing the lawn.

scenes.title: Discovery of the locked drawer
scenes.description: The narrator examines the furniture in her room and discovers that the lower drawer of an old chest of drawers is locked, preventing her from using it.

events.name: Holmes lectures Watson on literary style
events.description: Sherlock Holmes criticizes Watson's writing for focusing on sensationalism rather than the logical reasoning behind cases, advocating for a greater emphasis on his 'art' of deduction.

events.name: Holmes receives a new case letter
events.description: Holmes receives a crumpled letter dated from Montague Place, which he describes as his 'zero-point' and introduces a new situation for consultation.

events.name: Narrator's Flight and Encounter with Mr. Rucastle
events.description: An urgent telegram from HUNTER arrives, requesting Holmes's presence at the Black Swan Hotel in Winchester at midday the next day. | Despite the peculiar conditions outlined in the letter, Miss Hunter decides to accept the employment offer from Jephro Rucastle. | Holmes and the narrator look up train times in Bradshaw to plan their journey to Winchester, with Holmes deciding to postpone his chemical work. | Miss Hunter receives a letter from Jephro Rucastle offering her a governess position with unusual terms. | Miss Violet Hunter becomes the head of a private school. | Mr. Rucastle asks Miss Hunter to put on a specific electric-blue dress that is laid out in her room. | Mr. Rucastle privately explains that his elder daughter left for Philadelphia due to an aversion to her stepmother. | Mrs. Rucastle whispers something to her husband after breakfast on the third day of Miss Hunter's arrival. | Mrs. Toller enters the room and indicates she possesses significant knowledge about the situation, having been confined in the cellar. | Overcome by terror, the narrator flees the passage and runs into Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting outside and questions her about her fright. | The client expresses urgency to help the 'poor creature', and Holmes states they must wait until seven o’clock to act. | The fat man accuses Holmes and Watson of being thieves and spies, while Holmes questions him about his daughter. | The gentleman describes the child's peculiar amusement of killing cockroaches with a slipper, startling the narrator. | The narrator observes Mr. Rucastle emerging from a locked door in a seemingly uninhabited wing of the house, holding keys. | Toller, a servant, is observed to be drunk twice, which Mr. Rucastle seems to ignore. | Toller, having been drinking heavily, left the key in the door of the forbidden rooms, creating an opportunity for the narrator to gain access. | Violet Hunter arrives at Holmes's residence at the appointed time of half-past ten. | Violet Hunter explains her predicament and asks Holmes for guidance regarding a strange governess offer, as she has no family to consult. | Violet Hunter sends a letter to Holmes from Montague Place, expressing anxiety about a governess situation and requesting a consultation.

events.name: Client loses governess situation
events.description: The client's employment as a governess ends when Colonel Spence Munro moves to Halifax, Nova Scotia.

events.name: Client seeks new employment
events.description: The client advertises and answers advertisements, and regularly visits Westaway's agency, to find a new governess position.

events.name: Encounter with stout man at agency
events.description: During a visit to Westaway's agency, the client finds Miss Stoper with a 'prodigiously stout man' who observes the women seeking employment.

events.name: Job Interview for Governess Position
events.description: A gentleman offers the narrator a job, presenting it with an unusual custom of advancing half the salary. | A loud thudding noise is heard from downstairs at Copper Beeches upon the arrival of Holmes and his companions. | Mr. Rucastle takes Miss Hunter to an outhouse to show her his mastiff, Carlo, kept chained inside. | The initial performance of the peculiar ritual where Mr. Rucastle tells funny stories and expects the narrator to laugh heartily. | The narrator undergoes an interview for a governess position where the potential employer presents peculiar conditions, ultimately leading to the narrator's refusal and the end of the interview. | The narrator undergoes an interview for a governess position with an enthusiastic gentleman.

events.name: Offer of £100 Salary
events.description: The gentleman offers the narrator a salary of £100 a year for the governess position, which seems almost too good to be true.

events.name: Inquiry about Location and Duties
events.description: The narrator questions the gentleman about the job's location (Hampshire, The Copper Beeches near Winchester) and her specific duties, which involve caring for a single child.

events.name: Miss Hunter refuses job offer
events.description: Miss Hunter declines a job offer presented by Miss Stoper.

events.name: Miss Hunter reconsiders job offer
events.description: Facing financial hardship, Miss Hunter begins to regret her refusal of the job offer.

events.name: Miss Hunter receives a letter
events.description: Miss Hunter receives a letter from the gentleman who made the job offer, just as she was about to inquire about it again.

events.name: Miss Hunter receives employment offer
events.description: Miss Hunter receives a letter from Jephro Rucastle offering her a position with an unusually high salary and peculiar conditions.

events.name: Miss Hunter consults Holmes
events.description: Miss Hunter presents the suspicious employment offer to Mr. Holmes for his consideration and advice.

events.name: Client accepts employment and departs
events.description: Reassured by Holmes, the client decides to accept the unusual employment offer, sacrifice her hair, and travel to Winchester.

events.name: Holmes predicts future contact
events.description: Holmes predicts that they will hear from the client again soon, implying the situation will escalate.

events.name: Fortnight passes without news
events.description: Two weeks pass during which the narrator frequently thinks about the client's strange situation, wondering about the abnormality of her employment.

events.name: Holmes expresses need for data
events.description: Holmes impatiently states that he cannot make conclusions without sufficient data, comparing it to making bricks without clay.

events.name: Decision to travel to Winchester
events.description: The narrator and Holmes decide to take a train to Winchester.

events.name: Miss Hunter's journey to Copper Beeches
events.description: Holmes and the narrator travel by train to Winchester, passing through the English countryside. | Mr. Rucastle drove Miss Hunter in his dog-cart to the Copper Beeches.

events.name: Discussion on Crime in the Countryside
events.description: Holmes articulates his theory that the seemingly idyllic countryside can be a more dangerous place for hidden crimes than urban areas, due to isolation and lack of public scrutiny.

events.name: Narrator's Realization of the Forbidden Rooms' Mystery
events.description: A large, burly man appears at the door, interrupting Holmes's thoughts and initiating a confrontation. | A scream of agony and a horrible worrying sound are heard, indicating a violent attack by the unleashed dog. | After the incident with the man, Mrs. Rucastle instructs Miss Hunter to wave him away and then draws down the blind. | Holmes and Watson discuss the circumstances of the lady who has sought their help, noting that she is free to travel to Winchester to meet them, implying she is not under immediate personal threat. | Holmes discovers a long light ladder against the eaves, explaining how someone accessed the skylight. | Mrs. Rucastle catches Miss Hunter using the mirror and gives her a searching gaze, indicating she knows Miss Hunter saw something. | The fat man flees down the stairs, and an unfed dog is subsequently loosed, leading to an attack. | The mystery surrounding the sinister house with the copper beeches is fully solved. | The narrator finds a coil of hair identical to her own in a locked drawer, which she had opened out of curiosity. | The narrator finds a door that is locked and heavily barricaded from the outside with an iron bed bar, padlock, and stout cord. | The narrator hears steps and sees a shadow moving behind the barricaded door, causing her intense fear. | The narrator shoots and kills the attacking dog to save Rucastle. | The narrator took advantage of the opportunity to gently turn the key, open the door, and slip into the forbidden suite of rooms. | The narrator understood that there was something she was not to know about a suite of rooms, which ignited her determination to investigate. | Upon entering, the narrator found a little passage leading to three doors, with two of them opening into empty, dusty rooms.

events.name: Miss Alice meets Mr. Fowler
events.description: Miss Alice met Mr. Fowler at a friend's house, which subsequently led to her father's increased efforts to control her. | Miss Hunter meets Holmes and (implied) Watson at The Black Swan inn to seek their advice.

events.name: Arrival at Copper Beeches and Introduction to Family
events.description: The narrator is driven to Copper Beeches by her employer and introduced to his wife and child.

events.name: Rucastles' Exaggerated Delight
events.description: Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle express an exaggerated delight at Miss Hunter's appearance in the electric-blue dress.

events.name: Second Strange Ritual Performance with Reading
events.description: The repetition of the strange ritual two days later, which now includes the narrator being instructed to read aloud from a yellow-backed novel.

events.name: Order to Cease Reading and Change Dress
events.description: Miss Hunter is abruptly told to stop reading and change her attire, which she finds extraordinary and fuels her curiosity.

events.name: Miss Hunter Devises a Mirror
events.description: Miss Hunter, curious about what is being hidden from her, uses a piece of broken mirror and a handkerchief to create a way to see behind her.

events.name: Sighting of the Man in Southampton Road
events.description: Using her makeshift mirror, Miss Hunter sees a small bearded man in a grey suit looking towards the house from Southampton Road.

events.name: Questioning about the Man
events.description: Mrs. Rucastle and Jephro question Miss Hunter about the man she saw, implying suspicion and concern.

events.name: Man Stares at Miss Hunter
events.description: A man on the road stares up at Miss Hunter while she is sitting in the window. | Holmes, Watson, and the client arrive at the Copper Beeches house at seven o'clock, finding Miss Hunter on the door-step.

events.name: Miss Hunter Stops Sitting in Window and Wearing Blue Dress
events.description: Following the incident, Miss Hunter no longer sits in the window or wears the blue dress.

events.name: Warning about the dog
events.description: old Toller warns the narrator about the dangerous dog and advises her not to go outside at night.

events.name: Sighting of the giant dog
events.description: The narrator witnesses a giant, tawny-tinted dog, described as a 'dreadful sentinel', moving across the lawn at night.

events.name: Hair cut in London
events.description: The narrator had cut off her hair in London and placed it in a coil at the bottom of her trunk.

events.name: Discovery of the locked drawer
events.description: The narrator discovers a locked lower drawer in an old chest of drawers in her room, which she is unable to open.

events.name: Mr. Rucastle's angry demeanor and locking of the door
events.description: The narrator observes Mr. Rucastle emerging from a locked suite of rooms with an angry expression and locking the door, behaving uncharacteristically.

events.name: Narrator observes shuttered window
events.description: While walking in the grounds, the narrator notices that one of the windows of the mysterious suite is shuttered up, while others are merely dirty.

events.name: Mr. Rucastle's suspicious explanation
events.description: Mr. Rucastle explains the shuttered window by claiming it's his 'dark room' for photography, an explanation the narrator finds unconvincing.

events.name: Narrator's growing suspicion
events.description: The narrator's curiosity is aroused by Mr. Rucastle's behavior and explanation, leading to a strong sense of suspicion about the locked suite.

events.name: Narrator explores empty wing
events.description: The narrator enters the empty wing of the house, finding it lonely and eerie.

events.name: Man threatens narrator
events.description: The man threatens to throw the narrator to the mastiff if she enters the empty wing again.

events.name: Narrator decides to contact Mr. Holmes
events.description: Overwhelmed by fear of the household, the narrator resolves to send a wire to Mr. Holmes for advice.

events.name: Miss Hunter sends a wire
events.description: Miss Hunter sends a wire after making up her mind about her situation. | The narrator goes to an office located half a mile from the house to send a wire.

events.name: Miss Hunter goes to the office
events.description: Miss Hunter walks half a mile to the office and returns to the house.

events.name: Toller becomes insensible
events.description: Toller drinks himself into a state of insensibility, leaving him unable to control the dog.

events.name: Miss Hunter gets leave to come to Winchester
events.description: Miss Hunter obtains permission to travel to Winchester for the morning.

events.name: Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle plan a visit
events.description: Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are going on a visit and will be away all evening.

events.name: Holmes and the narrator listen to Miss Hunter's story
events.description: Holmes and the narrator listen spellbound as Miss Hunter recounts her adventures.

events.name: Holmes questions Miss Hunter
events.description: Holmes begins to interrogate Miss Hunter about details concerning Toller, the Rucastles, and the house's features.

events.name: Plan to incapacitate Mrs. Toller
events.description: Miss Hunter agrees to send Mrs. Toller into the cellar and lock her in to facilitate the investigation.

events.name: Holmes's Deduction on the Child's Disposition
events.description: Holmes explains his theory about the child's abnormal cruelty and its potential danger to the 'poor girl' to Watson and the client.

events.name: Miss Hunter provides keys
events.description: Miss Hunter gives Holmes the duplicate keys to Mr. Rucastle's, intended for the barricaded door.

events.name: Forcing the barricaded door
events.description: Holmes and Watson use their combined strength to break open the old, rickety door to the prisoner's room.

events.name: Discovery of the empty room
events.description: Upon entering the room, Holmes and Watson find it deserted, with the prisoner gone.

events.name: Holmes discovers the escape ladder
events.description: Holmes climbs onto the roof and finds a ladder against the eaves, revealing how the prisoner escaped through the skylight.

events.name: Dog Attack on Rucastle
events.description: A large, famished dog, intentionally loosed, attacks and severely injures Rucastle.

events.name: Mr. Rucastle's second marriage
events.description: Miss Alice's father married again, leading to Miss Alice's unhappiness at home.

events.name: Mr. Rucastle attempts to coerce Miss Alice
events.description: Mr. Rucastle tried to force Miss Alice to sign a paper to give him control over her money.

events.name: Miss Alice suffers brain-fever
events.description: Due to Mr. Rucastle's constant worrying, Miss Alice fell ill with brain-fever and was at death's door for six weeks.

events.name: Miss Alice's recovery and changed appearance
events.description: Miss Alice recovered from her illness, though she was worn to a shadow and had her beautiful hair cut off.

events.name: Mr. Fowler's continued loyalty
events.description: Despite Miss Alice's illness and changed appearance, Mr. Fowler remained loyal to her.

events.name: Mr. Rucastle implements imprisonment
events.description: Mr. Rucastle began a system of imprisonment for Miss Alice.

events.name: Miss Hunter brought from London
events.description: Mr. Rucastle brought Miss Hunter from London to deal with Mr. Fowler's persistent presence.

events.name: Mr. Fowler blockades the house
events.description: Mr. Fowler, being a persevering man, blockaded the house where Miss Alice was being held.

events.name: Marriage of Mr. Fowler and Miss Rucastle
events.description: Mr. Fowler and Miss Rucastle were married by special license in Southampton the day after their flight.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.description: A detective sitting in a great, old-fashioned chair, with a set purpose to avenge his client. | Annoyed by being identified as a detective, later anxious and despondent upon hearing the news. | Consulting detective examining a mysterious case. | Consulting detective, actively investigating the case and making preparations for an arrest. | Consulting detective, questioning the integrity of the crime scene. | Impatient, then anxious and decisive upon receiving news of the inscription. | Investigating the shooting, points out a crucial detail about a third shot. | Investigator examining the crime scene and making observations. | Investigator who is about to explain the case of the dancing men. | Leading the investigation with masterful progress. | Listened to the story with utmost attention and sat in silent thought. | Seated in silence, brewing a chemical product, and suddenly revealing knowledge of Watson's private thoughts. He then explains his method of deduction. | The consulting detective, who is presented with a new mystery. | The consulting detective, who is presented with the mysterious hieroglyphics. | The detective investigating the case, showing excitement about the new evidence. | The detective who makes a deduction about Watson's finances and introduces a new mystery. | The detective, offering advice to Hilton Cubitt. | The primary investigator, leading the examination of the crime scene. | Addressed by Inspector Martin, leading the investigation. | Consulting detective, offering his knowledge to ensure justice. | The companion of the narrator, who anticipated the crime. | The detective being addressed by Hilton, to whom the story is being recounted. | The detective investigating the case. | The detective listening to Mr. Hilton Cubitt's statement. | The detective to whom the narrator is speaking and seeking help. | The renowned detective, listening to his client's problem. | Engaged in an intricate calculation to decipher the meaning of the dancing men. | Investigating the circumstances of a shooting incident. | The consulting detective, thoughtful about the case of the dancing men. | The detective, maintaining a calm professional manner after the client leaves.

characters.name: Dr. Watson
characters.description: Astonished by Holmes's sudden intrusion into his intimate thoughts, he questions how Holmes knew. | Holmes's companion and the narrator. | Holmes's companion, who is present during the investigation and plans to accompany Holmes to town. | The narrator and companion of Sherlock Holmes. | The narrator, observing Holmes's work and awaiting his disclosures. | The narrator, present in the drawing-room with Holmes and the Inspector. | The narrator, whose financial plans are deduced by Holmes, and who reacts to the new mystery. | Holmes's friend and colleague who accompanied him to Norfolk. | Holmes's friend, present during the client's recounting of the case.

characters.name: Thurston
characters.description: An acquaintance of Watson with whom he plays billiards and who has an option on South African property.

characters.name: Mr. Hilton Cubitt
characters.description: A client who is worried about the mysterious 'dancing men' figures. | A client who previously consulted Holmes regarding the dancing men. | A gentleman from Riding Thorpe Manor, Norfolk, who is anxious about a conundrum and is coming to consult Holmes. | A person with whom the narrator had a second interview regarding the case. | A tall, ruddy, clean-shaven gentleman from Riding Thorpe Manor, Norfolk, who is anxious about a conundrum and seeks Holmes's help. | Shot at Riding Thorpe Manor, now dead. | Shot through the heart and deceased. | The client presenting a mysterious case to Holmes, from an old family in Norfolk. | The client who is narrating the events to Holmes. | The client who is presenting his case to Holmes, concerned about strange signals and an intruder. | The person who provided new material (two short sentences and one message) to Holmes. | A fine creature, a man of the old English soil, simple, straight, and gentle, with great, earnest blue eyes and a broad, comely face. He loves and trusts his wife, Elsie. | Sender of the letter, described as a 'simple Norfolk squire' entangled in a dangerous web. | The client, departing after his meeting with Holmes. | The person who sent Holmes the last message from Slaney. | The visitor who brought the case of the dancing men, whose departure prompts Holmes's intense study. | Found dead from a bullet wound, shot from the front. | Husband of Elsie and the narrator of this account, who accepted Elsie's terms regarding her past. | The person experiencing the mysterious messages and recounting the events to Holmes.
