crimes.name: Shooting of Mr. and Mrs. Hilton Cubitt
crimes.description: A conundrum involving absurd hieroglyphics on a sheet of paper, which Mr. Hilton Cubitt is anxious to understand. | A series of curious markings or absurd little figures appearing on a paper, which is frightening Mr. Hilton Cubitt's wife. | The appearance of mysterious 'dancing men' figures, which are a form of coded message or threat. | The central mystery involving the appearance of strange dancing figures that cause extreme fear and distress to Elsie. | The unsettling appearance of strange 'dancing men' figures and subsequent incidents causing distress to Mr. Hilton Cubitt. | A danger threatening Elsie, communicated through mysterious hieroglyphics, which Hilton Cubitt seeks Holmes's help to understand and resolve. | A series of mysterious 'dancing men' hieroglyphics are appearing, causing severe distress to the client's wife and threatening their peace. | A series of mysterious figures ('dancing men') that are the forerunners of a terrible tragedy. | Holmes is attempting to decipher the meaning of mysterious figures known as 'dancing men' that are causing annoyance to Hilton Cubitt. | The central mystery being investigated by Holmes, involving coded messages and recent dangerous events at Elriges Farm, leading to the anticipation of a dangerous prisoner. | A series of mysterious hieroglyphic messages appear, causing distress and leading to a vigil where a shadowy figure is seen. | An unusual case involving mysterious pencil markings on a torn page, presented to Holmes. | Mr. Cubitt was shot through the heart, resulting in instantaneous death. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt was shot through the heart and killed, while Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was shot through the brain and seriously injured. A pistol with two emptied barrels was found nearby. | The 'worst' event that had already occurred, with Abe Slaney being the suspected murderer. | The central enigma of the story, involving a series of peculiar symbols that convey a secret message, initially appearing as random sketches. | The central mystery involves deciphering the coded messages composed of dancing men symbols to understand their meaning and origin. | The central mystery involving strange signals and a skulking rascal appearing on Hilton Cubitt's property, causing distress to his wife.

crimes.name: Mystery of Elsie's Past
crimes.description: The central mystery surrounding Elsie's undisclosed and painful past associations, which resurfaces with a letter from America, causing her profound fear.

crimes.name: Threat to Elsie
crimes.description: A threatening inscription 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD' appeared on the sundial, indicating a dangerous situation for Elsie and Hilton Cubitt.

crimes.name: Shooting at Riding Thorpe Manor
crimes.description: A crime committed at three in the morning at Riding Thorpe Manor, described as a tragedy involving a 'most united couple'. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt was shot dead by his wife, who then shot herself and is now near death.

crimes.name: Murder of the master and assault on his wife
crimes.description: The master was found dead, and his wife was horribly wounded, after an explosion.

crimes.name: Murder of the unfortunate squire
crimes.description: The squire was shot from the front, the bullet penetrating his heart, causing instantaneous and painless death in his study.

crimes.name: Wounding of the lady
crimes.description: A lady was wounded by a bullet, requiring a serious operation.

crimes.name: Shooting incident at the house
crimes.description: An incident involving a firearm, a third person, and a bullet mark, referred to as 'the firing' and 'the tragedy'.

crimes.name: Shooting incident
crimes.description: The investigation into a shooting, focusing on the origin of a third bullet and related evidence.

crimes.name: Violent Incident at the Estate
crimes.description: The 'events of last night' involving a lady who may not recover consciousness, and the use of a revolver.

crimes.name: The Criminal Secret involving Abe Slaney
crimes.description: A hidden criminal matter suggested by the decoded messages, Abe Slaney's identity, and the lady's past.

objects.name: chemical vessel
objects.description: Holmes was brewing a particularly malodorous product in it.

objects.name: test-tube
objects.description: Holmes held a steaming test-tube in his hand and later propped it in a rack.

objects.name: check book
objects.description: Watson's check book, locked in Holmes's drawer, indicating he has not needed it for an investment.

objects.name: sheet of paper
objects.description: A paper containing an exact copy of the latest dancing-men hieroglyphics, presented to Holmes. | A paper from Holmes's notebook with curious 'dancing men' figures inscribed upon it, which Holmes studies intently. | A paper tossed by Holmes onto the table, containing absurd hieroglyphics or a 'child's drawing', which is the central mystery. | A piece of paper found on the sundial in the garden, bearing the dancing figures, which caused Elsie to faint. | A piece of paper on which the narrator copied the dancing men figures. | The material on which the hieroglyphic messages are copied or scrawled.

objects.name: paper with the curious markings
objects.description: A page torn from a notebook, marked in pencil with 'absurd little figures dancing across the paper', which later reveals 'AM-HERE-ABE-SLANEY'. It is the central clue.

objects.name: paper with markings
objects.description: A page torn from a notebook with mysterious pencil markings: AM-HERE-ABE-SLANEY. It is a key clue in the case.

objects.name: pocketbook
objects.description: Holmes's personal item where he carefully places the mysterious paper.

objects.name: letter from Hilton Cubitt
objects.description: A communication received by Holmes after a delay in the telegram's answer, updating him on the situation. | Communicates the appearance of a new inscription to Holmes. | A letter received by Elsie from America, which she immediately burned after reading, triggering her constant fear and distress. | The initial document that was the starting-point of all the trouble.

objects.name: American stamp
objects.description: A detail observed on the letter, indicating its origin from America, which was a sign of trouble.

objects.name: dancing figures
objects.description: Strange symbols resembling little dancing men, first found scrawled in chalk on window-sills and later on a paper found on a sundial, causing great alarm to Elsie.

objects.name: chalk
objects.description: The material used to scrawl the first set of dancing figures on the window-sills.

objects.name: pedestalled sundial
objects.description: A sundial with which the protagonists had strange associations. | An object in the garden where the paper with the dancing figures was discovered.

objects.name: hieroglyphics
objects.description: Symbols that evidently have a meaning, but the particular sample is too short and the facts too indefinite for immediate investigation. | The mysterious messages, including 'AT-ELRIGES' and 'COME-ELSIE', central to the mystery.

objects.name: wire from Hilton Cubitt
objects.description: A telegram sent by Hilton Cubitt to Holmes, indicating new and important incidents related to the dancing men.

objects.name: Papers of the dancing men
objects.description: Evidence possessed by Holmes related to the crime. | Mysterious stick figures arranged in a sequence, appearing on the door as a message or clue. | Mysterious hieroglyphics appearing as stick figures, central to the mystery and causing distress. | Various papers with figures of 'dancing men' recorded on them, which Holmes spreads out to discuss.

objects.name: hieroglyphics: AT-ELRIGES
objects.description: The specific sequence of dancing-men figures copied by the client from the tool-house door.

objects.name: revolver
objects.description: A firearm found on the floor midway between Mr. and Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, potentially the weapon used in the shooting. | A firearm taken by Hilton for protection during his vigil. | A weapon with an ejector, found at the scene. | The firearm used in the shooting, containing four cartridges, two of which were fired. | The implied firearm from which the third cartridge was ejected.

objects.name: pebble
objects.description: Used to hold down a message on the sundial.

objects.name: pistol
objects.description: The only firearm found in the room, with two barrels emptied, suggesting it was used in the shooting. | The weapon the narrator seized to confront the creeping figure.

objects.name: new dance
objects.description: A new, shorter arrangement of dancing men figures scrawled on the door.

objects.name: these papers
objects.description: Papers containing the strange 'dancing men' signals, which Holmes requests to study.

objects.name: slips of paper containing dancing men
objects.description: The primary clue in the case, used by Holmes for his calculations.

objects.name: long telegram
objects.description: A communication sent by Holmes after making progress in his calculations, hoping for an answer.

objects.name: long inscription
objects.description: A new instance of the dancing men figures that appeared on a pedestal, mentioned in Hilton Cubitt's letter.

objects.name: inscription
objects.description: A threatening message 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD' found on the pedestal of the sundial.

objects.name: time-table
objects.description: Used to check train schedules to North Walsham.

objects.name: cablegram
objects.description: A message received by Holmes, confirming the urgency of the situation.

objects.name: bullet
objects.description: One bullet killed Mr. Cubitt, another wounded the lady, and a third struck the window. | The projectile fired at the squire, which remained in his body after penetrating his heart. | The projectile that caused injuries to Mrs. Hilton Cubitt and killed Mr. Hilton Cubitt.

objects.name: a candle
objects.description: Burning upon the table in the study when the crime scene was discovered. | Its un-guttered state proved that the window and door were open for only a very short time.

objects.name: window
objects.description: The window in the study, found shut and fastened upon the inside. | The window in the study, which was shut and fastened upon the inside, a key detail for the crime scene. | Was open during the firing, allowing powder fumes to escape and a shot to be fired through it.

objects.name: dressing-gown
objects.description: Mr. Cubitt's garment, checked for powder-marking.

objects.name: cartridges
objects.description: Ammunition for the revolver; two were fired, four remain.

objects.name: window-sash
objects.description: Part of the window, hit by a shot from a third person outside. | The lower part of the window frame, where Holmes discovers a bullet hole, indicating a third shot.

objects.name: powder
objects.description: The smell of which indicated that the window and door were open during the firing.

objects.name: door
objects.description: Was open during the firing, contributing to the draught that cleared powder fumes.

objects.name: bullet mark
objects.description: Found on the window sash, confirming a shot was fired from outside.

objects.name: lady’s hand-bag
objects.description: A trim little handbag of crocodile-skin and silver found on the study table, containing money.

objects.name: twenty fifty-pound notes of the Bank of England
objects.description: Money found in a bag, deemed important for the upcoming trial. | The contents of the lady's hand-bag, held together by an india-rubber band.

objects.name: india-rubber band
objects.description: Used to hold the fifty-pound notes together inside the hand-bag. | Used to hold the fifty-pound notes together.

objects.name: bag
objects.description: A container holding the fifty-pound notes, handed to the inspector.

objects.name: third bullet
objects.description: A bullet found, whose trajectory indicates it was fired from inside the room.

objects.name: footmarks
objects.description: Large, masculine imprints with long, sharp toes found in the soft soil of the flower-bed.

objects.name: little brazen cylinder
objects.description: An object found in the grass, identified as the third cartridge from a revolver.

objects.name: cartridge
objects.description: The third cartridge found, related to the revolver.

objects.name: note
objects.description: A message Holmes wishes the stable-boy to take to Elrige's Farm. | A written message from Holmes addressed to Mr. Abe Slaney, dispatched via a young boy.

objects.name: slips of the dancing men
objects.description: Coded messages that Holmes is actively working to decipher, serving as a crucial clue in the investigation.

objects.name: Dancing Men symbols
objects.description: The coded characters that convey a secret message. They appear as figures, some bearing a flag and some not, which are hypothesized to indicate word breaks.

objects.name: symbols
objects.description: The coded messages in the form of dancing men figures, which Holmes is attempting to decipher.

objects.name: message
objects.description: A single word message provided by Mr. Hilton Cubitt, which Holmes analyzes.

objects.name: first message
objects.description: A coded message that the speaker is deciphering.

objects.name: second message
objects.description: Another coded message that the speaker is deciphering.

objects.name: message from Slaney
objects.description: A message sent by Slaney to Hilton Cubitt, deciphered by Holmes, which read 'ELSIE .RE.ARE TO MEET THY GO.' with added 'P' and 'D' indicating threats.

deductions.observation: groove between your left forefinger and thumb
deductions.inference: You had chalk between your left finger and thumb when you returned from the club last night. You put chalk there when you play billiards, to steady the cue. You never play billiards except with Thurston. You told me, four weeks ago, that Thurston had an option on some South African property which would expire in a month, and which he desired you to share with him. Your check book is locked in my drawer, and you have not asked for the key.
deductions.conclusion: You do not propose to invest your money in this manner.

deductions.observation: absurd little figures dancing across the paper upon which they are drawn
deductions.inference: it would appear to be some childish prank

deductions.observation: These hieroglyphics have evidently a meaning.
deductions.inference: If it is a purely arbitrary one, it may be impossible for us to solve it. If, on the other hand, it is systematic, I have no doubt that we shall get to the bottom of it.
deductions.conclusion: The solvability of the hieroglyphics depends on whether they are arbitrary or systematic.

deductions.observation: This particular sample is so short and the facts which you have brought me are so indefinite.
deductions.conclusion: We have no basis for an investigation at this moment.

deductions.observation: The new drawing of dancing men was on a different panel of the door, not merely an addition to the first.
deductions.inference: This indicates a separate message or a significant change in the communication.
deductions.conclusion: This information is crucial for solving the mystery and provides hope for a breakthrough.

deductions.observation: The inscription 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD' has appeared on the sundial, and Hilton Cubitt is entangled in a 'singular and a dangerous web'.
deductions.inference: The situation has escalated to a critical and life-threatening point, requiring immediate intervention.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes and Watson must travel to North Walsham without delay.

deductions.observation: Holmes points to a hole which had been drilled right through the lower window-sash, about an inch above the bottom.
deductions.inference: The bullet struck the edge of the window.
deductions.conclusion: A third shot has been fired, and therefore a third person must have been present.

deductions.observation: servants said that on leaving their room they were at once conscious of a smell of powder
deductions.inference: It suggested that at the time of the firing, the window as well as the door of the room had been open. Otherwise the fumes of powder could not have been blown so rapidly through the house. A draught in the room was necessary for that.
deductions.conclusion: Both door and window were only open for a very short time, however.

deductions.observation: the candle was not guttered
deductions.inference: Because the candle was not guttered (implying a long draught would have guttered it).
deductions.conclusion: Both door and window were only open for a very short time.

deductions.observation: Feeling sure that the window had been open at the time of the tragedy
deductions.inference: I conceived that there might have been a third person in the affair, who stood outside this opening and fired through it. Any shot directed at this person might hit the sash.
deductions.conclusion: I looked, and there, sure enough, was the bullet mark!

deductions.observation: the window to be shut and fastened
deductions.inference: The woman’s first instinct would be to shut and fasten the window.
deductions.conclusion: The window was shut and fastened by the woman.

deductions.observation: splintering of the wood
deductions.inference: The third bullet has clearly been fired from inside the room.
deductions.conclusion: The shot originated from within the room.

deductions.observation: Mrs. King's testimony that she was awakened by a 'loud' explosion, and the question of whether it seemed louder than the second one.
deductions.inference: It might have been two shots fired almost at the same instant.
deductions.conclusion: It was undoubtedly so (two shots fired almost simultaneously).

deductions.observation: The flowers were trampled down, and the soft soil was imprinted all over with footmarks. Large, masculine feet they were, with peculiarly long, sharp toes.
deductions.inference: Someone with large, masculine feet and peculiar toes was present in the flower-bed.
deductions.conclusion: The presence of these distinct footmarks indicates a specific individual's movement outside the window.

deductions.observation: A little brazen cylinder found in the grass.
deductions.inference: The revolver had an ejector, and here is the third cartridge.
deductions.conclusion: The third cartridge from the weapon used in the shooting has been recovered.

deductions.observation: The revolver had an ejector, and here is the third cartridge.
deductions.conclusion: Our case is almost complete.

deductions.observation: Holmes works with the 'slips of the dancing men' and considers 'all that happened here during the night'.
deductions.inference: Holmes has successfully deciphered the dancing men code and understood the sequence of events, identifying the perpetrator and their location.
deductions.conclusion: Mr. Abe Slaney is the dangerous individual responsible for the recent events, and his apprehension is imminent.

deductions.observation: The 'singular productions' (dancing men figures) are a form of secret writing.
deductions.inference: The system was invented to conceal that the characters convey a message, making them appear as random sketches of children.
deductions.conclusion: This form of cipher is entirely new to Holmes, despite his extensive knowledge of secret writings.

deductions.observation: these characters convey a message
deductions.inference: applied the rules which guide us in all forms of secret writings
deductions.conclusion: the solution was easy enough

deductions.observation: Out of fifteen symbols in the first message, four were the same
deductions.inference: E is the most common letter in the English alphabet, and it predominates to so marked an extent that even in a short sentence one would expect to find it most often.
deductions.conclusion: it was reasonable to set this down as E.

deductions.observation: in some cases the figure was bearing a flag, and in some cases not
deductions.inference: it was probable, from the way in which the flags were distributed, that they were used to break the sentence up into words.
deductions.conclusion: I accepted this as a hypothesis, that flags were used to break the sentence up into words.

deductions.observation: The order of the English letters after E is by no means well marked, and any preponderance which may be shown in an average of a printed sheet may be reversed in a single short sentence. Speaking roughly, T, A, O, I, N, S, H, R, D, and L are the numerical order in which letters occur, but T, A, O, and I are very nearly abreast of each other
deductions.inference: it would be an endless task to try each combination until a meaning was arrived at.
deductions.conclusion: I therefore waited for fresh material.

deductions.observation: In the single word message, two E’s come second and fourth in a word of five letters.
deductions.inference: The word could be ‘sever,’ ‘lever,’ or ‘never.’
deductions.conclusion: ‘never’ is the most probable word as a reply to an appeal, and circumstances suggest it was written by the lady.

deductions.observation: Appeals came from someone intimate with the lady in her early life, and a combination of symbols contained two E’s with three letters between.
deductions.inference: This combination might stand for the name ‘ELSIE.’
deductions.conclusion: Such a combination formed the termination of a message repeated three times, confirming it was an appeal to ‘Elsie.’

deductions.observation: The word preceding ‘Elsie’ had only four letters and ended in E.
deductions.inference: Holmes tried all other four-letter words ending in E but found none to fit the case.
deductions.conclusion: The word must be ‘COME.’

deductions.observation: The word must be ‘COME’ after trying all other four letters ending in E and finding none to fit the case.
deductions.inference: By eliminating other possibilities for words ending in 'E', 'COME' is the only fit.
deductions.conclusion: Possession of C, O, and M for further decoding.

deductions.observation: The partially decoded message: .M .ERE ..E SL.NE.
deductions.inference: The first letter can only be A, occurring three times, and H is apparent in the second word.
deductions.conclusion: The message reads: AM HERE ABE SLANEY.

deductions.observation: The partially decoded second message: A. ELRI. ES.
deductions.inference: Putting T and G for missing letters makes sense, suggesting a house or inn name.
deductions.conclusion: The message refers to a house or inn where the writer was staying.

deductions.observation: Abe is an American contraction, and a letter from America was the starting-point of the trouble.
deductions.inference: The name 'Abe' combined with the origin of the initial letter points to American nationality.
deductions.conclusion: Abe Slaney was an American.

deductions.observation: The lady’s allusions to her past, and her refusal to take her husband into her confidence.
deductions.inference: These behaviors indicate a hidden aspect or problem.
deductions.conclusion: There was some criminal secret in the matter.

deductions.observation: Slaney trying to escape ('To fly')
deductions.inference: If he attempts to escape, it implies he is guilty.
deductions.conclusion: To fly would be a confession of guilt.

scenes.title: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's Arrival and Presentation of the Paper
scenes.description: A worried and depressed client arrives at Mr. Holmes's residence, describing the distress caused by the mysterious 'dancing men' hieroglyphics to himself and his wife, and presents a copy of the latest message. | After Hilton Cubitt leaves, Holmes intensely studies the slips of paper containing dancing men, performing intricate calculations for two hours. | Hilton Cubitt arrives from Norfolk, looking worried and depressed, and expresses his distress over the ongoing 'dancing men' business to Holmes. | Hilton Cubitt concludes his statement, expressing his anger at his wife for holding him back from confronting an intruder and his suspicion about her true fears. He then asks Holmes for advice, suggesting a violent confrontation. Holmes advises against simple remedies and asks for the papers, promising a visit. | Hilton Cubitt leaves, and the narrator observes Holmes's hidden excitement despite his calm demeanor. | Hilton recounts Elsie's pre-marital confession about her painful past, his acceptance of her terms, their happy marriage, and the recent incident where Elsie received and burned a letter from America, leading to her constant fear. | Hilton recounts finding a third message on the sundial and his decision to lie in wait in his study with a revolver. | Hilton's wife interrupts his vigil, and together they observe a dark figure moving near the tool-house. | Holmes and Inspector Martin begin a thorough examination of the study, finding the squire's body, noting his disordered dress, and confirming he was shot from the front, resulting in instantaneous death. | Holmes and Watson discuss the impending visit of Mr. Hilton Cubitt and the 'little conundrum' he is bringing. | Holmes and Watson embark on a seven-mile carriage ride to Riding Thorpe Manor, during which Holmes is silent and deeply despondent. | Holmes calls Watson back, informing him that Hilton Cubitt has sent a wire indicating new important incidents, and is expected to arrive soon. | Holmes deduces the presence of a third person firing from outside and finds a bullet mark on the window sash, confirming his theory. | Holmes examines the paper with the dancing figures, makes an initial assessment, and Mr. Cubitt explains his wife's terror. | Holmes explains to Inspector Martin his deductions about the open window and door during the firing, based on the smell of powder and the un-guttered candle. | Holmes expresses satisfaction with his progress, discusses the case with Watson, and sends a telegram, anticipating a trip to Norfolk. | Holmes finds and examines a lady's hand-bag containing twenty fifty-pound notes on the study table. | Holmes instructs the stable-boy to saddle a horse and take a note to Elrige's Farm. | Holmes is impatient for news, then receives a letter from Hilton Cubitt detailing a new, threatening inscription on the sundial. | Holmes meticulously analyzes the dancing men symbols, using letter frequency and contextual clues to decipher key words like 'NEVER', 'ELSIE', and 'COME', making significant progress in understanding the coded messages. | Holmes presents Watson with a sheet of paper containing strange hieroglyphics, introducing a new, unexplained problem from Mr. Hilton Cubitt, who is expected to arrive soon. | Holmes questions the narrator about the placement of the new dancing men drawing, showing excitement and concluding its importance. | Holmes reacts with dismay to the inscription, realizes the extreme urgency of the situation, and decides to travel to North Walsham immediately, confirming this with a cablegram. | Holmes recounts his actions leading up to the current situation, including cabling Wilson Hargreave about Abe Slaney, receiving a reply, deciphering a threatening message from Slaney to Hilton Cubitt, and his subsequent journey to Norfolk with Dr. Watson, only to find that 'the worst had already occurred'. | Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Mr. Hilton Cubitt discuss the mysterious markings on a torn page, which Holmes examines carefully. | Holmes, Inspector Martin, and the narrator are inside the room, examining the origin of the third bullet and questioning Mrs. King about the sounds of the explosion. | Holmes, Inspector Martin, and the narrator move to the garden, discover distinctive footmarks in the flower-bed, and Holmes finds a crucial brazen cylinder (cartridge). | Holmes, while engrossed in a chemical experiment, suddenly reveals his knowledge of Watson's private thoughts about South African securities, astonishing Watson. Holmes then begins to explain his general method of deduction. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt arrives at Baker Street, is described, and immediately draws attention to the paper with the curious markings, explaining its impact. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt begins to recount his personal story, starting with his marriage to Elsie Patrick in London. | Saunders and Mrs. King recount being aroused from sleep by explosions, then descending to find their master dead and his wife severely wounded in the study, which was filled with smoke and the smell of powder. | Sherlock Holmes advises Mr. Hilton Cubitt to return to Norfolk, observe, and collect more evidence regarding the dancing men, as the current information is insufficient for an investigation. | The narrator explains the initial process of deciphering the Dancing Men code, recognizing the symbols as letters, identifying 'E' through frequency analysis, and hypothesizing that flags indicate word breaks. He notes the difficulty in proceeding without more material due to the variability of letter frequencies in short texts. | The servants describe finding the room full of smoke and powder, the window fastened, their mistress injured, and their belief that no one could have escaped the house. They also mention noticing the smell of powder from the top floor.

scenes.title: Holmes's Deduction on Watson's Finances
scenes.description: Holmes explains his detailed deduction to Watson regarding his decision not to invest in the gold fields, based on a series of logical inferences. | The local surgeon reports on Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's serious but not fatal injuries and Mr. Hilton Cubitt's death, noting the bullet was discharged at close quarters.

scenes.title: Narrator recounts events to Mr. Holmes
scenes.description: The Norfolk squire explains to Mr. Holmes the strange occurrences involving his wife Elsie and the mysterious dancing figures, seeking his help.

scenes.title: Hilton Cubitt consults Holmes
scenes.description: Hilton Cubitt explains his concerns about his wife Elsie and the mysterious hieroglyphics to Holmes, who listens attentively and offers initial advice and an assessment of the limited evidence.

scenes.title: Presentation of Second Hieroglyphics
scenes.description: Hilton presents Holmes with a copy of a second hieroglyphic message, 'COME-ELSIE', which appeared two mornings later. | Hilton presents Holmes with a copy of the first hieroglyphic message, 'AT-ELRIGES'. | The narrator presents a copy of the newly discovered dancing men figures to Holmes.

scenes.title: Confrontation at the Tool-House
scenes.description: The narrator's wife sees a creeping figure near the tool-house in the moonlight. The narrator attempts to confront it with a pistol but is held back by his wife. Upon reaching the door, the figure is gone, but a new set of dancing men is found.

scenes.title: Waiting for the Telegram and Cubitt's Letter
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson wait impatiently for an answer to the telegram, but instead receive a letter from Hilton Cubitt detailing a new inscription.

scenes.title: Arrival at North Walsham Station
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham, where the station-master informs them of the tragic shooting at Riding Thorpe Manor. | Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham, where they are met by the station-master.

scenes.title: Journey to Norfolk and Arrival at Riding Thorpe Manor
scenes.description: The narrator describes the singular countryside of East Anglia and the Norfolk coast during their journey, culminating in their arrival at Riding Thorpe Manor, noting its features like the tool-house and sundial.

scenes.title: Encounter with Inspector Martin and Discussion of the Crime
scenes.description: Inspector Martin arrives in a dog-cart, introduces himself, and expresses astonishment at Mr. Holmes's early presence at the crime scene. Holmes explains he anticipated the crime and mentions the 'dancing men' as his evidence.

scenes.title: Holmes Questions Scene Integrity
scenes.description: Holmes questions the Doctor and the constable about whether anything at the crime scene was moved or touched. | Holmes, the country surgeon, and Inspector Martin are examining the room where Mr. Cubitt was murdered and a lady wounded, discussing the bullet wounds and the absence of powder-marking. Holmes then discovers a bullet hole in the window-sash, indicating a third shot and a third person. | Mr. Holmes offers his assistance to the inspector, who agrees to collaborate on the investigation.

scenes.title: Identifying the Alarm Raiser
scenes.description: Holmes asks who sent for them and learns it was the housemaid, Saunders.

scenes.title: Investigation in the Hall
scenes.description: Holmes, Watson, Inspector Martin, the country doctor, and a village policeman gather in the old hall, which has been turned into a court of investigation, to hear testimonies regarding the incident.

scenes.title: Investigation with Inspector Martin
scenes.description: Holmes and Inspector Martin discuss the case, examining the revolver and cartridge, with Martin expressing admiration for Holmes's progress.

scenes.title: Questioning Servants about Elrige's
scenes.description: Holmes questions the servants about a place called 'Elrige's', with the stable-boy providing a lead to 'Elrige's Farm'.

scenes.title: Holmes Prepares for Apprehension
scenes.description: Holmes works on the dancing men slips, writes a note to Mr. Abe Slaney, and dispatches a boy to deliver it. He then advises the Inspector to prepare for a dangerous prisoner and plans to leave for London with Watson.

scenes.title: Instructions for Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's Visitors
scenes.description: After the note is dispatched, Holmes gives specific instructions to the servants regarding how to handle any visitors who inquire about Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, emphasizing secrecy about her condition.

scenes.title: Retreat to the Drawing-Room
scenes.description: Holmes leads the way into the drawing-room, remarking that the immediate business is now out of their hands.

scenes.title: Holmes Prepares to Explain the Dancing Men Case
scenes.description: In the drawing-room, Holmes, Watson, and the Inspector are present. Holmes prepares to explain the mystery of the dancing men, displaying the relevant papers and referencing his prior consultations with Mr. Hilton Cubitt.

scenes.title: Explanation of Code-Breaking and Deductions
scenes.description: The speaker details his process of deciphering the dancing men code, identifying Abe Slaney, and inferring a criminal secret, to Inspector Martin.

scenes.title: Discussion with the Inspector in Norfolk
scenes.description: An inspector expresses concern to Holmes about Abe Slaney potentially escaping, given that he is suspected of murder. Holmes reassures the inspector that Slaney will not try to escape and expects him to arrive, revealing he has written to Slaney.

events.name: Holmes reveals knowledge of Watson's thoughts
events.description: Holmes surprises Watson by stating his private thoughts about investing in South African securities, causing Watson great astonishment.

events.name: Holmes explains his deductive method
events.description: Holmes lectures Watson on the general principle of constructing a series of simple inferences to reach a startling conclusion.

events.name: Holmes deduces Watson's financial intentions
events.description: Holmes reveals his deduction that Watson has decided against investing his capital in the gold fields, based on a chain of observations and inferences.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt's Account of His Wife's Fear
events.description: A dark, creeping figure is seen moving in the shadow of the tool-house. | A lady's hand-bag containing a significant sum of money is found on the study table, becoming a crucial piece of evidence. | A new arrangement of dancing men figures is found scrawled on a different panel of the door. | The client found a fresh crop of dancing men drawn in chalk upon the black wooden door of the tool-house. | Hilton Cubitt recounts his wife's fear when he tried to confront the intruder, initially suspecting she feared for the intruder, but ultimately concluding she feared for his safety. | Hilton agrees to marry Elsie on her own terms, content to take a woman who will remain silent about her past. | Holmes presents a sheet of paper with 'absurd hieroglyphics' to Watson, introducing a new mystery that a client, Mr. Hilton Cubitt, is anxious about. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt presents a page with strange pencil markings to Holmes, initiating the investigation. | The client describes his and his wife's severe distress due to the mysterious dancing men messages. | The client unfolds a paper with an exact copy of the hieroglyphics for Holmes to examine. | The discovery of the name 'Abe Slaney' through the decoded messages. | The master is found dead, lying upon his face in the center of the study. | The master's wife is found horribly wounded and unable to speak, crouching near the window in the study. | The narrator realizes the limitations of frequency analysis for short texts and the difficulty of further deciphering the code without additional material. | The narrator successfully identifies the symbol for 'E' in the Dancing Men code using frequency analysis and forms a hypothesis about the use of flags. | The station-master informs Holmes and Watson about the shooting of Mr. Hilton Cubitt and his wife at Riding Thorpe Manor. | The unfortunate squire is found dead in his study, shot through the heart.

events.name: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's impending visit
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt, the sender of the mysterious paper, is expected to arrive by the next train to consult Holmes.

events.name: Arrival of the 'little conundrum'
events.description: The mysterious paper with the dancing figures arrives by post at Holmes's residence.

events.name: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's visit to Baker Street
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt arrives at Holmes's residence to seek help with the mysterious markings.

events.name: Revelation of the dancing men figures
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt presents the paper with the curious markings to Holmes for examination. | The narrator finds absurd little dancing figures scrawled with chalk on the window-sills.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt's Marriage to Elsie Patrick
events.description: Holmes and Watson begin their seven-mile carriage journey to Riding Thorpe Manor. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt recounts meeting and marrying Elsie Patrick in London during the Jubilee. | Upon receiving the news of the inscription and a cablegram, Holmes determines the situation is critical and decides to travel to North Walsham immediately.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt's Initial Consultation
events.description: A worried client arrives at Holmes's residence by hansom. | Elsie reveals to Hilton that she has had very disagreeable associations in her life and wishes to forget them, setting conditions for their marriage regarding her past. | Following the letter incident, Elsie lives in constant fear, with a look as if she were waiting and expecting something. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt consults Sherlock Holmes about the mysterious 'dancing men' figures appearing at his home.

events.name: Elsie Receives and Burns Letter from America
events.description: Elsie receives a letter with an American stamp, turns deadly white, reads it, and immediately throws it into the fire, marking the beginning of her constant fear.

events.name: Elsie's serious reaction to figures
events.description: The narrator's wife, Elsie, reacts very seriously to the mention of the dancing figures and asks to see any future occurrences.

events.name: Discovery of paper with dancing figures
events.description: The narrator finds a paper with dancing figures lying on the sundial in the garden.

events.name: Elsie faints upon seeing the paper
events.description: Elsie drops in a dead faint after being shown the paper with dancing figures.

events.name: Narrator sends paper to Mr. Holmes
events.description: The narrator writes to and sends the paper with dancing figures to Mr. Holmes for help.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt seeks Holmes's help
events.description: Hilton Cubitt consults Holmes regarding a danger threatening his wife Elsie, which is connected to mysterious hieroglyphics.

events.name: Holmes's initial assessment of the hieroglyphics
events.description: Holmes examines the hieroglyphics and the available facts, concluding that more information is needed before a full investigation can commence.

events.name: Holmes Receives Wire from Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Sherlock Holmes receives a telegram from Hilton Cubitt indicating new, important developments regarding the dancing men.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt Arrives at Baker Street
events.description: Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham and are greeted by the station-master. | Holmes and Watson arrive by train at North Walsham station. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt arrives at Holmes's residence, visibly distressed by the ongoing incidents related to the dancing men. | The protagonists arrive at Riding Thorpe Manor, the location of the recent crime.

events.name: Holmes and Martin Examine the Study
events.description: Holmes and Inspector Martin begin their investigation by thoroughly examining the crime scene in the study. | The client saw the man who draws the dancing men at his work. | The process of breaking the coded messages, leading to the identification of key letters and words.

events.name: Second Hieroglyphic Message Appearance
events.description: A message reading 'AT-ELRIGES' appears, prompting Hilton to make a copy. | A shooting incident occurred, leaving a smell of powder and a bullet mark, indicating a third person's involvement. | A threatening inscription, 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD', appears on the sundial at Riding Thorpe Manor. | Hilton Cubitt asks Holmes for advice on how to deal with the intruder and the strange signals, suggesting a violent confrontation. | Hilton Cubitt leaves Holmes's residence to return home, observed by the narrator. | Hilton and his wife observe a dark figure moving in the shadow of the tool-house during the vigil. | Hilton decides to lie in wait in his study with a revolver to catch the perpetrator. | Hilton's wife appears in his study during his vigil, imploring him to come to bed. | The action of sending a cable to Wilson Hargreave of the New York Police Bureau for further investigation. | Three days later, a message with characters similar to the last one is found under a pebble on the sundial. | Two mornings later, a fresh inscription reading 'COME-ELSIE' appears.

events.name: Holmes Requests Papers and Promises Visit
events.description: Holmes advises against simple remedies, requests the papers with the signals, and promises to visit Hilton Cubitt's home soon to investigate further. | Inspector Martin of the Norfolk Constabulary arrives and is astonished to find Mr. Holmes already at the scene of the crime.

events.name: Holmes performs intricate calculation
events.description: Sherlock Holmes dedicates two hours to an elaborate calculation based on the slips of paper with dancing men.

events.name: Holmes sends a telegram
events.description: After making progress, Holmes writes and sends a long telegram related to the case.

events.name: Letter from Hilton Cubitt arrives
events.description: Following a delay in the expected telegram answer, a letter arrives from Hilton Cubitt, reporting a new inscription.

events.name: Holmes Reveals 'Dancing Men' Evidence
events.description: Holmes deduces that the four-letter word preceding 'ELSIE' in the message is 'COME'. | Holmes identifies a repeated sequence of symbols that spells 'ELSIE', indicating an appeal to the lady by that name. | Holmes successfully deciphers a five-letter word from the symbols as 'NEVER', concluding it is a probable reply from the lady. | Mr. Holmes states that he possesses 'the evidence of the dancing men' regarding the crime. | The servants provide their account of the immediate aftermath of the crime, including the state of the room, the injured mistress, and the fastened doors.

events.name: Inspector Martin agrees to collaborate with Holmes
events.description: Inspector Martin accepts Mr. Holmes's offer to associate in the investigation.

events.name: Surgeon reports on victims' condition
events.description: The local surgeon provides details on Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's serious injuries and Mr. Hilton Cubitt's fatal wound.

events.name: Crime scene details revealed
events.description: It is noted that the bullet was discharged at close quarters and a pistol with two emptied barrels was found.

events.name: Holmes questions scene handling
events.description: Holmes interrogates the Doctor and Constable about any alterations made to the crime scene.

events.name: Housemaid Saunders identified as alarm raiser
events.description: Holmes discovers that Saunders, the housemaid, was the one who called for help.

events.name: Arrival at the Crime Scene
events.description: Holmes, Watson, Inspector Martin, the country doctor, and a village policeman arrive at the house to investigate the incident.

events.name: Testimony of Saunders and Mrs. King
events.description: The housemaid Saunders and the cook Mrs. King recount their discovery of the master's body and his wounded wife after hearing explosions.

events.name: Discovery of the third bullet hole
events.description: Holmes points out a bullet hole in the window-sash, revealing that a third shot was fired, implying the presence of a third person.

events.name: Discovery of the fifty-pound notes
events.description: Holmes finds twenty fifty-pound notes in a bag, which are deemed important for the trial.

events.name: Investigation of the third bullet's origin
events.description: Holmes examines the splintered wood to determine that the third bullet was fired from inside the room.

events.name: Questioning Mrs. King about the explosion
events.description: Holmes interrogates Mrs. King about the loudness of the explosion she heard, leading to a deduction about simultaneous shots.

events.name: Discovery of footmarks in the flower-bed
events.description: Large, masculine footmarks with peculiar toes are found in the trampled flower-bed outside the study window.

events.name: Discovery of the third cartridge
events.description: Holmes finds a little brazen cylinder in the grass, identifying it as the third cartridge from the revolver.

events.name: Holmes declares case almost complete
events.description: Holmes informs Inspector Martin that the investigation is nearing its conclusion based on the evidence.

events.name: Holmes questions servants about Elrige's
events.description: Holmes seeks information about a specific location, 'Elrige's', from the household staff.

events.name: Stable-boy identifies Elrige's Farm
events.description: A stable-boy remembers a farmer named Elrige and points towards 'Elrige's Farm' near East Ruston.

events.name: Holmes sends note to Mr. Abe Slaney
events.description: Holmes dispatches the stable-boy with a message to the newly identified 'Elrige's Farm'. | Holmes sends a letter to Abe Slaney, asking him to come to their location. | Holmes writes and dispatches a note to Mr. Abe Slaney at Elriges Farm via a young boy, with strict instructions for its delivery.

events.name: Holmes advises Inspector on prisoner
events.description: Holmes advises the Inspector to telegraph for an escort, anticipating the need to convey a particularly dangerous prisoner to the county jail.

events.name: Holmes gives instructions for Mrs. Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Holmes instructs the servants not to reveal Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's condition to visitors, but to show them into the drawing-room.

events.name: Holmes begins to explain the Dancing Men case
events.description: Holmes draws his chair to the table, spreads out the papers with the dancing men, and prepares to recount the circumstances of the case to Watson and the Inspector, referencing his previous consultations with Mr. Hilton Cubitt.

events.name: Second Interview with Mr. Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt provides Holmes with additional coded messages, including two short sentences and a single word. | The narrator mentions an upcoming second interview with Mr. Hilton Cubitt, indicating a continuation of the investigation and the expectation of new information.

events.name: Inference of a Criminal Secret
events.description: The realization that the messages and the lady's behavior point to an underlying criminal secret.

events.name: Holmes cables Wilson Hargreave
events.description: Holmes sends a cable to his friend at the New York Police Bureau to inquire about Abe Slaney.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt sends last message
events.description: Hilton Cubitt sends a message from Slaney to Holmes, which Holmes then deciphers.

events.name: Holmes and Watson arrive in Norfolk
events.description: Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to Norfolk, arriving after 'the worst had already occurred'.

events.name: The 'worst' occurs
events.description: A grave event, implied to be a murder, takes place before Holmes and Watson's arrival in Norfolk.
